Let's make this concrete. You've been paying $1,800/month in rent for the past year, diligently hitting your five monthly transactions. Your Bilt account holds approximately 21,600 points (1x on rent, plus some bonus earning on the card). You're planning a long weekend in Nashville with your partner.

The Property: Hyatt Place Nashville Downtown. Category 3, costing 12,000 World of Hyatt points per night. Cash rate for a Friday–Sunday stay: $189/night, totaling $378 for two nights before taxes and fees. With taxes, you're looking at roughly $430 out of pocket.

The Points Play: Transfer 24,000 Bilt points to Hyatt instantly, book two nights. Total points spent: 24,000. Total cash paid: $0 (Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges, no award fees).

The CPP calculation: $378 cash value ÷ 24,000 points = 1.58 cents per point at the conservative end. Factor in the taxes you're also avoiding (most properties don't charge taxes on award stays), and your effective CPP climbs closer to 1.8–2 cents per point.

Now scale up. Apply the same 24,000 points to a single night at Park Hyatt Chicago — a Category 7 property. Cash rate: $550–$700/night on a peak weekend. Points cost: 30,000 per night (you'll need to save a couple extra months). At $600 cash value for 30,000 points, you're at 2 cents per point — but if you hit a $700 night, that's 2.33 cpp.

The experience itself? Park Hyatt properties deliver: floor-to-ceiling windows, complimentary minibar items, a spa, and a level of service that genuinely doesn't feel like a "points hotel." You're not using a coupon at a budget chain — you're staying at the same property business travelers expense at full rate, experiencing everything they experience, funded almost entirely by the rent check you wrote anyway.

If you hold Hyatt Globalist status, suite upgrades on award stays are available based on availability — turning a 30,000-point redemption into a $900+ suite night. That's where the CPP ceiling of 8 cents per point becomes real.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

World of Hyatt awards include a fifth-night-free benefit on standard award redemptions when you book five or more consecutive nights. On a five-night stay at a Category 5 property (20,000 points/night), you'd normally pay 100,000 points — but with the fifth night free, it's 80,000 points for five nights. That's a 20% improvement in value with zero extra effort. Plan longer trips to unlock this.

Do: Book 395 Days Out for Peak Destinations

Hyatt opens award inventory at the same time as cash inventory — 395 days in advance. For high-demand properties (think Park Hyatt Maldives at Hadahaa or Alila Ventana Big Sur), availability at standard rates disappears quickly. Set a calendar reminder and search early.

If you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, your Chase Ultimate Rewards points also transfer to Hyatt at 1:1, instantly. This means you have two separate point pools feeding the same program — Bilt for rent earnings and Chase for everyday spending. Together, you can accumulate Hyatt points significantly faster and take on higher-category properties.

Avoid: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability

Bilt-to-Hyatt transfers are instant and irreversible. If you transfer 30,000 points and then can't find the availability you thought you saw, those points are now in Hyatt — and if you don't use them, they expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Always search Hyatt first, confirm dates and property, then transfer.

Avoid: Missing the 5-Transaction Monthly Minimum

This is the most common Bilt mistake. If you forget to make five purchases on your Bilt card in a given month, you earn zero points on rent — not reduced points, zero. Automate five small recurring charges to the card and never think about it again.

Do: Target Category 4–6 Properties for Best Value

Category 1–3 properties offer solid value, but the CPP accelerates meaningfully in Categories 4–6 (15,000–25,000 points/night) where cash rates are $200–$400 but points costs haven't kept pace. This is the sweet spot within the sweet spot.

Do: Watch for Hyatt's Points + Cash Awards

Hyatt offers a Points + Cash option at roughly half the standard award rate, combined with a cash co-pay. If your Hyatt balance is small, this lets you access properties without waiting to accumulate a full award.

This redemption was built for renters — specifically, renters who are already on the path to FI and feel the friction of paying rent every month with nothing to show for it. If you pay at least $1,000/month in rent, this sweet spot is generating meaningful Hyatt points from dollar one. At $2,000/month, you're accumulating 24,000 Hyatt points per year from rent alone — enough for two nights at a Category 5 property or a single aspirational night at a Park Hyatt.

Minimum to make it work: You need at least 5,000 Hyatt points for a Category 1 redemption — easily achievable after 5–6 months of rent payments on a $1,000/month lease. For aspirational Category 6–7 stays, you're targeting 25,000–30,000 points, which takes planning but is absolutely achievable.

This isn't the right fit if you own your home (no rent to earn on), if you're already deep into a competing hotel loyalty program, or if your primary travel goal is international business class flights — in that case, transferable airline currencies deserve more of your attention first. But for hotel stays, especially in the U.S., this is the single most frictionless on-ramp into the Hyatt ecosystem available anywhere.

This redemption earns a **5/5 for beginner friendliness**, and that rating is accurate — but it helps to understand exactly *why* it's easy, so you don't accidentally make it harder than it needs to be. **What makes it easy:** - Earning is passive. Once your Bilt card is set up and rent is registered, points accrue automatically with no behavior change required (beyond five small monthly transactions). - The transfer is instant — no waiting, no uncertainty, no risk of availability disappearing while points are in transit. - Hyatt's award chart is fixed and transparent. You can see exactly what a property costs before you transfer a single point. - No fuel surcharges means no unpleasant surprises at checkout. **The one area that trips beginners up:** forgetting the five-transaction monthly minimum. This is the single most common Bilt mistake, and it's entirely preventable. Set up five small autopay charges on your Bilt card — a $5 streaming service, a recurring Amazon purchase, anything — and you'll never miss it. **Tip for the first redemption:** Start with a Category 3 or 4 Hyatt Place or Hyatt Regency for a domestic weekend trip. The points requirement is low (8,000–15,000 points), availability is widely open, and the booking process is identical to any other Hyatt stay. It's a low-stakes way to see the entire system work from earning to booking. If you can pay rent, own a smartphone, and make five purchases a month, you can execute this redemption. The ChooseFI community has embraced this one for good reason — it's genuinely the most accessible entry point into premium hotel travel rewards available today.

No. Bilt works with any landlord that accepts payment. If your building is not in the Bilt Alliance, Bilt processes the payment via ACH. The only difference is Alliance buildings may offer additional perks like bonus points or rent credits.

You will still pay your rent through Bilt, but you will earn zero points on that month's rent payment. The five-transaction requirement resets monthly. Set up autopay on small recurring charges to prevent this.

Yes. Bilt transfers to over a dozen airline and hotel partners including American Airlines, United, Air Canada Aeroplan, and IHG. However, Hyatt consistently delivers the highest cents-per-point value among hotel transfer partners.

Bilt caps rent earning at 100,000 points per month (equivalent to $100,000 in rent at 1x). For the vast majority of renters, this cap is irrelevant. There is no annual cap on total points earned.

The Bilt-to-Hyatt pipeline is the most accessible travel rewards sweet spot available today. You are already paying rent. The Bilt card has no annual fee. Hyatt points deliver 2-8 cents in value. The transfer is instant. If you rent and you are not earning Hyatt points from that rent payment, you are leaving hundreds of dollars in annual hotel value on the table. Start with one Category 3-4 weekend stay to see it work, then scale up to aspirational properties as your balance grows.

#8952. The Latest and Greatest Sunglasses for Triathletes, Tested in Training and Racing

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Sunglasses and triathletes go hand in hand. With not one but two sports calling for a good pair, and after so much time spent nitpicking over the perfect goggles, we can’t settle for less when it comes to shading our eyes through the bulk of our training and racing.

It’s not just about UV protection and keeping bugs and debris out, because, let’s be honest: style matters, too. And today’s saturated performance sunglasses market offers a nearly unlimited selection of styles, with many pairs more high-tech and often higher-priced than ever before.

We wanted to get a clearer, less-tinted picture of the triathlon-worthy sunglasses landscape in 2026, so we combed the internet to see what was on the cutting edge and spent the summer testing a wide range of pairs while running and cycling across different terrains and climates.

Along the way, we explored the latest tech, picked out standout features, and figured out what felt worth the money – and what wasn’t quite there yet. From light-shifting photochromic lenses and video-recording AI smart glasses to everyday pairs that won’t break the bank, here’s our roundup of the best sunglasses for triathletes in 2026.

In the Pacific Northwest where I live, it can be raining one minute and sunny the next. A ride might take you from wide-open roads into dense, dark forests, sometimes around a single corner. For that reason, I’ve found light-shifting lenses incredibly useful. But even if you don’t live where I do, these glasses are practical in plenty of other changing light conditions, such as an early-morning long ride that starts before the sun comes up and ends well into the day.

One of the biggest drawbacks of traditional photochromic sunglasses is that the lenses don’t always adjust as quickly as the light changes. Their tint range also has limits, and they don’t always get as clear or as dark as you’d like. Most rely on UV light to darken, which means they may not respond as you’d expect behind a UV-blocking windshield in your car or when you’re testing them by a window before heading outside.

That’s a perfect segue into where we’ll start, as the first pair on our list looks to address these issues by taking a different approach: tint you control with a swipe.

One of the most intriguing pairs on this entire list comes from a new brand called Povec. Rather than waiting for the lenses to react to changing light, these glasses allow you to swipe an interface on the temple to change the tint in about a second.

Sure enough, I was surprised by just how quickly, and how dramatically, the tint changed. It started shifting as soon as we swiped the temple, so naturally, we spent the next several days playing with it back and forth. The electrochromic tech, as it’s called, worked so well that the glasses quickly became a showpiece for impressing friends.

These glasses ironically shone in dimmer conditions, especially when we went off-road or deep into the forests and needed to change the tint quickly. When mountain biking, being able to change the tint almost immediately as we rounded a corner into a dense forest descent felt invaluable.

At the same time, we were slightly less impressed with the optical quality in harsher light. There are subtle but apparent reflections, and the clarity is just a little off. It’s nothing dramatic, but it is noticeable, especially compared with the crystal-clear optics of some other glasses on this list.

Our favorite everyday pair of photochromic sunglasses, especially for spring and fall days in the PNW forests, was the SunGod Velans 2.

This ultralight pair offered some of the best optical clarity, field of view, and comfort of any glasses on this list, even before the added bonus of photochromic lenses. They shifted from light to dark quickly enough for our normal riding, although they couldn’t match the on-demand tint changes of the Povecs.

SunGod has become increasingly visible in triathlon thanks to athletes such as Hayden Wilde and Chelsea Sodaro donning them, but also because of a few appealing extras not often found elsewhere in the market. An array of customization options, an emphasis on durability, repairability, and recycled packaging, and a lifetime guarantee that includes repairs for accidental breakage make the higher price easier to digest. Furthermore, features such as replacement lenses and screwless hinges make the price more logical and suggest this pair will likely last you for the long term rather than just a couple of seasons.

Tifosi consistently makes it into our roundups for offering quality sunglasses at some of the best prices, and its light-shifting options are no exception.

We tried the Rail XC with Clarion Blue “Fototec” lenses, which offer a stated light-transmission range of 12% to 46%.

Compared with the SunGods, these felt like only a small step down in optical quality and fit during our testing. We did notice more glare from sunlight at certain angles and slightly more fogging during humid runs. At 31 grams, they were also a little heavier.

But beyond that, there’s little else to nitpick. They’re comfortable, clear, and transition smoothly and quickly, with nose pads and temple tips that adjust on the fly, offering plenty of room to dial in comfort.

Perhaps the most controversial pair on this list, these smart glasses have divided opinions about where this technology belongs in triathlon. From Ironman banning their use at its events to T100 welcoming them through a partnership, it’s a hot topic.

After training and racing in them twice, my own mixed opinion comes down to something simpler: I thoroughly enjoy wearing them and appreciate their practicality, but I’m still struggling with the bulky styling of the Vanguard. Enough so that I often intentionally leave them behind so I’m not the guy with the video sunglasses when running or cycling with friends.

That functionality, on the other hand, is hard to argue with. Being able to capture hands-free video and photos, listen to music, take phone calls, and ask Meta questions — among many other features — makes these glasses useful in ways a regular pair simply can’t match.

The Oakley Prizm lenses offered the clarity we expected, although the bulkier frame slightly restricted the field of view. Even after keeping them in their case and using only a microfiber cloth to clean them, I also noticed tiny scratches under close inspection after a few months of use. They weren’t noticeable while wearing the glasses, but they were there.

At 66 grams, you’ll notice the weight, too. If you have one of the lightweight alternatives on this list sitting next to them, you might think twice before grabbing these for an everyday session.

Where these really earned their place is in documenting your triathlon experiences. At SOS Triathlon and Escape from Alcatraz, capturing moments before, during, and after the race felt almost effortless. I could quickly tell Meta to take a photo or record a video, then download the footage to my phone through the app afterward, and I was set. Compared with previously having to bring GoPros, set up shots, and worry about batteries and SD cards, it makes it all too easy.

On the way to the SOS check-in tent, I even asked Meta to help me remember the different stages of this unique multi-stage race (read more about the SOS here).

Like it or not, smart glasses are likely to become an increasingly familiar sight around triathletes. After using them, I can understand the appeal.

Read a full Oakley Meta Vanguard review here.

The award for the most pleasantly surprising sunglasses on this entire list goes to this Oakley Meta rival, which packed in enough features to put the Vanguard on the ropes.

I’ll admit I went into testing the Rover sunglasses with the preconceived notion that these wouldn’t compete with the powerhouse name above. But I was taken aback by both the quality and functionality.

The first things I noticed were the weight, more than 10 grams lighter than the Vanguard, and the lenses. I hadn’t expected optics this good from a brand I had never heard of.

Then it only got better. The Rovers offer both landscape and portrait recording, plus a tiltable camera that helps you adjust the shot. The video resolution was also better than I expected at 3K and 60 fps – all capabilities the Vanguard doesn’t offer.

One of the standout features was the intercom function, which lets the glasses act like a walkie-talkie with fellow cyclists using the BleeqUp app. Being able to talk to each other more easily is something I’ve always wanted on small group rides, and hearing everyone clearly through the sunglasses themselves takes away the hassle of phone calls or dealing with headphones.

They’re marketed as AI sunglasses, with tools for quickly editing captured footage and adding ride-data overlays. If you’re feeling extra AI-adventurous, you can also generate a third-person view of your ride using mapping data and an uploaded photo of yourself and your bike. The results were interesting, to say the least.

Where the Rovers fell slightly behind the Vanguards was in the polish. The interface, AI assistant, and connectivity didn’t feel as refined as Meta’s. The feedback sounds weren’t as distinct, and connecting the glasses could be a little confusing, with frequent requests to reconnect to their Wi-Fi.

The Vanguard also comes with a charging case, which simplifies things, while the Rover uses a magnetic USB charger. Finally, having to say “Hey Bleeker” to activate the assistant just felt super weird.

One final gripe: The temples could rub against the lenses when folded, which felt like a small but frustrating design oversight.

In contrast to the pleasant surprise of the BleeqUp Rovers, these heads-up display sunglasses fell well short of my expectations.

I was excited to see whether technology similar to what we’ve enjoyed in Form’s smart swim goggles could bring the same benefit to running and cycling. Unfortunately, I was disappointed from the moment I unboxed them.

The idea is great, but the execution wasn’t there. The fit was the least comfortable of any glasses on this list, sitting unusually high on my face, and the secondary inner lens that houses the HUD projection compromised the view.

The bright green data displayed on the inner lenses is intended to keep cyclists from having to look down at their bike computer so they can focus on what’s ahead. In practice, however, I found the view even more distracting, sometimes struggling to adjust my focus from what I was reading on the glasses back to the road.

It was less of an issue while running, and thankfully, you can adjust the brightness and make some changes to the display position to keep the data less intrusive, but that was little consolation.

The app also felt unfinished, and we experienced several issues trying to connect our devices. Top it off with the worst-sounding built-in speakers and most robotic voice assistants I’ve heard in a while, and I’ll sadly be leaving HUD glasses out of my periphery for a while.

If I had the budget and could choose just one everyday pair to wear everyday or bring on a trip, like our recent all-in Ironman World Championship coverage, I’d choose the Oslo 2.0.

The blend of aesthetics, lens quality, and fit is hard to beat. Grippy temple tips and a very grippy nosepiece (which comes in various sizes) help it transition easily from casual use to training. Although it doesn’t look like it’s meant for running, it performs as well as a pair designed specifically for the sport.

For cycling, though, I prefer a little more lens coverage. That’s where I’d reach for Roka’s San Remo Air, which offers a similarly understated cafe style, but with more coverage and a vented lens for hot days.

Both were pairs I could happily wear all day, and all night if I had to. They also had some of the fewest fogging issues while running in the heat and humidity of a Washington summer and felt among the most premium of the bunch — from the finish of the frames to the cases they came in.

Our favorite mid-priced everyday pair was the Adidas Kaphiros, which came surprisingly close to the Rokas in overall performance. It also became the pair my wife consistently stole – sorry, “borrowed” – before we headed out for a ride together.

These are truly glasses you forget you’re wearing. They almost feel like they float above your ears. If pressure around your ears is something that regularly bothers you — as it has for me in the past — this is the pair I’d recommend.

The lenses offer generous coverage for cycling protection, and the optical quality impressed me. Small openings in the temples let air through while riding, although the glasses tended to fog during hot, humid runs — likely due to the size of the lenses.

Tifosi makes this list for a second time, beating out plenty of other running and cycling sunglasses as our favorite budget everyday pair.

The Vogel XC is lightweight, has proved durable enough to survive a couple of seasons with me, and offers a rimless, vented design that’s hard to beat at this price.

The lens tint we tested hit a useful middle ground for the varied conditions we wore it in. And the size and shape don’t scream “I’m a triathlete” every time you wear them out in public.

#8951. Does Breathing Deeply Feel Hard? Yoga Can Help.

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about deep breathing first appeared in the March-April 2004 issue of Yoga Journal. You can find more of our Archives here.

With each breath you take, a symphony of muscular activity occurs. As you inhale, some muscles contract while others relax. The result is an expanded space for the lungs, and thus for the breath. As you exhale, the space you need to breathe shrinks—again, through a complex set of muscular actions. For smooth and effective breathing to take place, the muscles involved in the breathing deeply must be fine-tuned and coordinated, just like the instruments of an orchestra.

The lungs don’t have the power to expand and contract on their own: They are inflated by air pressure to the size of their container, the rib cage. The rib cage in turn is expanded or compressed by the surrounding muscles. The breath orchestra includes many different muscles in the chest, back, neck, and abdomen, but none are as important as the diaphragm, which plays a primary role in expanding the breathing space during inhalation and helping control the shrinkage during exhalation.

You can visualize the diaphragm as half a basketball that attaches all the way around the lower ribs. When the diaphragm relaxes, it arches up toward the heart. When it contracts, it becomes flatter, pushing down toward the abdomen. Most of the sensation you feel when you inhale comes from the outward expansion of the belly and lower ribs, a movement created by the contraction of the diaphragm. This contraction lengthens the space available for the lungs and expands the rib cage to the front, the back, and the sides, causing air to be drawn into the lungs. When you exhale, the reverse happens: The diaphragm relaxes, arching up again; your belly becomes flatter; and the rib cage shrinks, pushing the air back out.

Anything that restricts the movement of the diaphragm restricts the breath, especially limiting the ability to inhale fully. There are many conditions that can constrict the diaphragm, including wearing overly tight clothes or a belt cinched too snugly around the waist. Another common cause is slumped posture. Sit up tall and notice how the lower ribs lift up off the abdomen and the adjacent upper belly becomes spacious. Now slump forward, letting your spine round back and your head jut forward. In this position, you’ll feel the lower ribs dig back and in toward the spine, compressing the diaphragm and the upper belly.

Retaining the space your diaphragm needs to move freely is only one of the many reasons it’s a good idea to work on your everyday posture; it’s also a good reason to be conscious of your spinal alignment in seated forward bends. If you work too aggressively to get your head toward the floor in these poses, your spine will round backward and your diaphragm will become compressed.

The movement of the diaphragm can also be restricted by tightness in the abdominal muscles. Pain or fear can lead to gripping in this area; combine that with holding your breath—another common habitual response to anxiety—and you have a recipe for an all-but-immobilized diaphragm. The abdominals can also become overly tight and short through too much focus on abdominal strengthening exercises like curl-ups and crunches.

Each time you curl your head and chest off the floor, you recreate a slumped position and train the abdominals to pull the lower ribs down toward the navel and back toward the spine. If the abs are never given a counterbalancing stretch, they will constantly hold the ribs in that constricted position.

Now don’t get me wrong. I absolutely believe that the ab muscles must be kept strong and conditioned. Their strength is important in supporting the abdominal organs and lower back. It’s also needed to compress the abdomen, assisting in exhalation, and for such forceful exhalations as coughing, sneezing, and fast breathing during exercise.

So the abdominal muscles need to be strong enough to perform their jobs, but they should not be so short, tight, and rigid that they restrict lung expansion and limit inhalation. The upper abdominals, which are strengthened during curl-ups and crunches, are the guilty gang that can put the squeeze on the diaphragm. These upper abdominals include the upper fibers of the rectus abdominus, which sits lengthwise in the center of the abdomen, running between the pubic bone below and the lower sternum and the rib cartilage above. The external and internal obliques, which cross the abdomen diagonally like a supporting girdle, also have upper fibers that attach to the lower ribs and can restrict rib cage movement.

To return to the musical analogy, rigid and short abdominals can overpower the rest of the breath orchestra and limit the contribution that other muscles—especially the diaphragm —can make to the symphony of the breath. Besides disturbing the proper balance between the different muscles involved in breathing deeply, and thus disturbing the breath’s rhythm, tight upper abdominals can contribute to chronic neck pain and headaches. When the expansion of the lower lung space is restricted, we tend to compensate by over-expanding the upper lung space. In this situation, the muscles that lift the rib cage and expand the space between the upper ribs—including the sternocleidomastoid muscles (on the front of the neck) and the upper trapezius muscles (on the back of the neck)—have to do much more than their usual share of the work during inhalation. Neck strain and chronic neck tension are often the result. And the most common cause of headaches is neck tension, especially the excessive pull on the base of the skull where the upper trapezius attaches.

To keep your obliques and rectus abdominus in optimal working order, you must train them to relax and lengthen as well as to contract and shorten. You can begin this process simply by taking a few moments after abdominal strengthening exercises or poses to invite the abs to relax.

Lying on your back, place your hands on your belly, with your fingers spreading out below your navel. When you inhale, your diaphragm will contract and push down on your belly, which will expand under your hands. This upward and outward expansion indicates that the abdominals have released and are lengthening

The abdominal muscles will lengthen even more if you recline over a bolster.

With your hips on the floor, lie back on the bolster so your torso and head are supported, your arms are relaxed out to the sides, and your chest is open. If you position the end of the bolster just at the bottom of your ribs, you’ll lengthen the upper abdominals and create space for the diaphragm. Now take a few minutes to breathe slowly and steadily, feeling the expansion of each inhalation as it gets drawn down into the lower rib cage and upper belly

Along with this exercise, many backbends can help stretch the abs, including Camel Pose (Ustrasana), Upward-Facing Bow Pose (Urdhva Dhanurasana), and Bridge Pose (Setu Bandha Sarvangasana).

If your diaphragm has been limited for years by snug waistbands, tight ab muscles, slumped posture, or habitual breath-holding, it may be too out of condition to contribute much to the breathing process. You can strengthen the diaphragm by providing some resistance to its work. Lying on your back, place some weight on your belly.

The appropriate weight will vary according to your size and ability, from one to two pounds (perhaps a bag of rice) to eight to 10 pounds (a yoga sandbag) or even more. But it should always be something that is soft and can spread, so it will sit comfortably in place. As your belly expands each time you inhale, the diaphragm will have to work harder to lift the extra weight.

Breathe slowly for a few minutes, working for a smooth breath pattern.

With practice, you can create an appropriate balance in the muscles of your belly—a balance that allows them to relax as your diaphragm contracts during inhalation yet keeps them strong enough to support the lower back and assist in exhalation. As your awareness of the diaphragm increases, you may find yourself opting for looser clothes and for seated and standing positions that don’t compress your belly. You may also begin to notice when you respond to stress, anger, and other emotions by holding your breath and tightening your abdomen—and realize that your tension melts away when you release your grip, allowing your diaphragm to move and your breath to flow. After all, the smooth, beautiful music of the breath is not just an important focus in yoga and meditation; it can help you stay centered and calm even as the storms of life rage around you.

#8949. The Swedish Sport of Swimrun Is Spreading Across the U.S. I Tried It and Chaos Ensued.

Outside features editor Frederick Dreier participated in the October 4 Ötillö Swimrun race at Horsetooth Reservoir, Colorado. Dreier has competed in triathlons, bicycle races, and other endurance sports for 25 years.

A few memories come to mind from my recent Ötillö Swimrun, the endurance race that combines open-water swimming with trail running.

In one, I flounder in the chilly waters of Colorado’s Horsetooth Reservoir near Fort Collins, my arms feeling heavy as concrete as I struggle to swim in a straight line. In another, I sit by the side of a rocky trail plucking cactus spines out of my backside, moments after a clumsy toe-strike sent me tumbling into a clump of prickly pear.

Both of these scenes, however, are superseded by a memory with an altogether different vibe. That, of course, is crossing the finish line and exchanging a flurry of high-fives and hugs with a bunch of random sweaty strangers, all of us clad in wetsuits, goggles, and running shoes.

You see, I had a blast racing my first Ötillö Swimrun race despite the dead-tired arms and cactus butt.

If you have never heard of the swimrun racing format, here’s a quick primer. Picture a triathlon, minus the biking. Now, chop up the swimming and running portions, stitch them together in smaller portions, and spread the whole event out on a point-to-point course. You run, then swim, then run again, then swim, and so on. The event I did was a “sprint” distance event, comprised of five swims and six runs spread out across 12 miles of trails and lake.

It took me nearly three hours to complete, and at no point was I sprinting.

Unlike triathlon, where you abandon your gear after each portion, swimrun requires you to carry all of your stuff from start to finish. Thus, you must swim while wearing your running shoes, run while clad in your wetsuit, and carry your pull buoy, hand paddles — swimming gear that is allowed — for the entire journey. This makes for some hilarious blunders along the way (more on this later).

Within the swimrun world, Ötillö is the proverbial Ironman — the most recognizable brand of events. Outside has a somewhat rich history of chronicling the Swedish company, first in 2013, then in 2014, and also in a 2017 Brad Stulberg column. In 2019, longtime contributor W. Hodding Carter wrote an Outside feature story about his foibles at the Ötillö world series race in Cannes, France, where he and his partner paddled across the green-blue Mediterranean and jogged through the French Riviera.

In all of those stories, Ötillö swimrun races come across as grueling, fun, and distinctly European. The racing format, after all, was developed in Sweden and first held on the chain of islands just east of Stockholm, which is still the site of the annual Ötillö world championships. The name “Ötillö” is a Swedish word that loosely translates to “island to island.”

Good news for Americans: Ötillö is no longer just for the Euros. In 2023, the series expanded to North America after it purchased a budding collection of U.S. swimrun races called the Odyssey series, that were co-founded by a guy named Lars Finanger. Finanger and I were roommates in Boulder 20 years ago, back when we were both dirtbag triathletes chasing a daily endorphin high.

Now, Finanger is trying to spread the Swedish swimrun gospel in the U.S., where jogging trails while wearing a wetsuit is about as popular as pickled herring.

“We started out with a lot of triathletes, Ironman finishers, Eco-Challenge racers — it was a really eclectic group of endurance athletes,” Finanger told me. “Now we have a small but dedicated following of athletes who see themselves as Swimrunners first, even though they might do a triathlon or a bike race, too.”

Finanger first learned about Ötillö from the 2013 Outside story. He was burned out on triathlon and road bike racing and was looking for a new challenge, so he signed up for the world championship event in Stockholm, which is comprised of 38 miles of running and 5.7 miles of swimming, and requires participants to compete in teams of two. It’s a grueling test of endurance and grit that takes many teams upwards of 10 hours to complete.

“I had this big grin on my face throughout the whole thing, even though the water was so frickin’ cold and the trails made you feel like you were running through the hobbit scene from Lord of the Rings,” Finanger told me. “I realized we didn’t have anything like it in the USA.”

Finanger wanted to start his own race but didn’t know how. As luck would have it, he wasn’t the only person intrigued by the format. Jeffrey Cole, a veteran of the endurance sports industry and a longtime triathlon race director, emailed Finanger about the swimrun format. Cole said that Casco Bay, Maine, near his home in Kennebunkport, was a perfect place to recreate the island hopping of Sweden’s Ötillö. In 2016, they started the inaugural Odyssey event along the Maine coast.

“I think about the history of triathlon, where athletes raced in Kona and then went back home to put on their own races where they lived,” Finanger said. “We wanted to produce a swimrun that we’d have wanted to do ourselves.”

Their model was a success. Finanger and Cole started other swimrun races in the U.S.: Orcas Island, Washington; Cedarville, Michigan; Austin, Texas; and even one on California’s Catalina Island. These events are held annually, and the participation numbers now surpass 400 at some races.

Cole died in 2018, and Finanger kept the business going alongside a handful of new partners. In 2023, Ötillö approached them about purchasing the Odyssey series and bringing it under the corporate umbrella. Finanger said it was a no-brainer.

“It meant partnering with the gold standard in our sport,” he said.

These days, the former Odyssey races award points to elite athletes that help them qualify for the world championships race in Stockholm. But they also boast shorter distances, solo categories, and a laid-back vibe. Because the purpose of the events, Finanger told me, is to attract newbies like yours truly to the format.

“We are still this meeting ground for all of these different types of athletes — swimmers, cyclists, triathletes,” he said. “The one they have in common is they are adventure-minded.”

Qualifying for a race in Europe was not on my mind as I prepared for the 2026 Colorado Ötillö. The shorter sprint distance did not offer qualification points toward the Ötillö World Championship; however, the much longer World Series race in Colorado (23 total miles) did.

When I asked Finanger for strategic advice, he just laughed me off. “Just have fun out there, dude,” he said. He reminded me that the whole point was to have a personal adventure while swimming and jogging my way around the lake.

The laid-back atmosphere at the start line reinforced Finanger’s advice. Over the years, I’ve nervously waited for the start of Ironman triathlons, marathons, and almost every type of bike race out there. At Ötillö, the vibe was extremely chill — like what you’d expect at the start of a 5K color run or a boozy bicycle parade and not a three- to five-hour test of stamina.

Still, I had to remind myself to have fun more than a few times during the early moments of the race. Following a fast one-mile run to start the race, we plunged into Horsetooth Reservoir for the first swim.

I’m a former NCAA Division III swimmer and multiple Ironman finisher, and I’m accustomed to swimming in choppy water filled with thrashing arms and legs. But I struggled to find my groove with the swimrun gear, and I had to stop a few times to position my pull buoy between my legs and learn to swim while wearing sneakers. An even bigger challenge hit when I exited the water.

I stepped onto the clay beach and immediately stumbled around like a newborn fawn. I felt like I’d just gulped a tequila shot or three. I lumbered toward the trail and zigzagged my way up a hill like a punch-drunk boxer.

Upon exiting the water, seasoned swimrunners fastened their pull buoys to their waists with a cord, tucking the apparatus to their lumbar sections like a fanny pack. I fumbled to secure mine as I trotted along, the buoy bouncing off of my butt. As I twisted and twirled the buoy, one of my plastic swim paddles slipped from my hand, and I heard it crash into a bush. Should I stop to look or keep going? I wondered. I chose to stop.

The short pause allowed my thumping heart rate to chill. Soon, my brain fog cleared, and I was able to focus. I found the paddle, and as I jogged along the trail, I familiarized myself with the goofy gear. I practiced tucking and untucking my pull buoy into its tether. I threaded the fingers of my right hand through the elastic loops on my hand paddles to keep them secure.

During a triathlon, you’re constantly using products that are over-engineered for the specific modality of the moment: aerodynamic bike stuff, cushioned shoes, high-visibility swim goggles. Part of the fun quirk of a swimrun is learning to manage the wrong gear when it’s not used for the right job.

My confidence increased, and I picked up the pace, jogging past swimrunners and moving to the side as others jogged past me. People seemed stoked to be on the trail. Nobody seemed so caught up in their own struggles as to skip the customary “Lookin’ good!” or “Go get ’em!” during a pass.

The sprint course deviated from the World Series route near the five-mile mark, and I bid adieu to the athletes who were tackling the longer distance. I saw a handful of sprint racers up ahead of me and decided to push my pace on a long switchback ascent to try and catch them.

Perhaps it was my soaring body temperature inside my wetsuit, or my lingering buzz. But as I closed in on the guy ahead of me, my mind wandered, and I tripped on a rock, completed a somersault, and landed in the cactus. Bewildered, I made a mental note about swimrun: shit can hit the fan if you don’t pay attention.

The fall meant that I had to spend a few minutes plucking spines from my backside once I crossed the line. But the ordeal delivered one of my lasting takeaways from the race.

Perfection does not exist during a swimrun. Even during a shorter distance race, you’re bound to inhale water, drop your gear, battle through exhaustion, or trip and stumble. How you deal with these setbacks defines your experience out there.

I’ve spent the last 25 years trying out different endurance sports. And I’m familiar with the progression that most athletes follow with these sports. You try out a sport and fall in love with the adventure, camaraderie, and community. Then, as the years go by, you focus more on your results, and before you know it, you’re completing a training regimen, following a performance-oriented diet, and dreaming of a top-10 finish.

I will absolutely compete in another Ötillö Swimrun event, but I don’t envision myself ever getting too hardcore about the format. Simply doing a swimrun gave me enough feeling of adventure and carefree silliness, without an ounce of self-seriousness. Sucking at the format provided half of the joy. And I’m more than happy to chase that feeling again.

#8947. I Took Marijuana Edibles to Find Out If Weed Makes You Faster—Or If It Just Feels That Way

The ride felt easier and more immersive—find out if the data told a different story.

I still remember my first time in Colorado after weed was legalized. I walked into a dispensary and my mind was blown by the very chill and knowledgeable manager at the shop walking me through all the strains available. He pointed out the anticipated vibes around each one and which were the best options for activities like rides and trail runs.

Marijuana use in outdoor sports is not new, but efforts to study its effect on performance have been gaining steam. Everyone from the University of Colorado Boulder to the Gatorade Sports Science Institute is putting resources into how this substance impacts endurance sports.

More states have legalized recreational marijuana and many cyclists I’ve talked to have asked whether there are performance benefits or risks. While there are several helpful studies on the effects of marijuana on endurance athletes, none focus on cycling.

With few specific answers available, I wanted to put together my own test. Since I live in New Jersey, a state where recreational weed is legal, I bought a pack of edibles from a local dispensary and gathered all of the sensors I have available. Then I put together a simple study. In the safety of my own home, I would jump on Zwift, following the same route before and after taking edibles. The location was important. While research on marijuana’s impact on cycling performance is rare, multiple studies have shown that THC can impair coordination and slow reaction times, two factors that can increase the risk of cycling, especially outside the relatively controlled environment of my home trainer setup.

To keep outside variables in check, I rode the trainer through Zwift’s Loopin Lava route. I chose this route because I wanted something less than 60 minutes (including warmup and cooldown) that had sustained climbing sections as well as some flat and rolling sections to get a bit of variety. In all, it has about 690 feet of climbing over 11.5 miles.

I aimed to average about 185 watts (roughly zone two) on both tests—keeping my power output the same on both rides, I hoped, would reveal something about weed’s effects on my workout.

My home lab felt like it was made for this moment. As a health and fitness editor at Bicycling, and longtime fitness industry professional, I’ve been growing my collection of sensors for years—I was using a Garmin heart-rate sensor, a power meter built into the Wahoo trainer, a CORE temperature sensor, a Nix sweat sensor, and I used a pulse oximeter to check my oxygen saturation levels in 10-minute intervals. These sensors gave me insight into things I was curious about for the test—I even used my Coros Pace 4 as a backup. Does heart rate change? How does sweat rate and sweat content change after some gummies? Does internal body temperature or oxygen saturation rise or fall after a little weed? I was about to find out.

I did my baseline ride first, then took about a 90-minute break to let my internal temperature reset and let my body reset. Once I finished my first ride I took 40 milligrams of marijuana edibles and gave them some time to kick in (yes, that’s a relatively large dose; I wanted to make sure I experienced the full effects of the edibles on my riding in this not-too-scientific test).

I pulled all the data through Strava, the CORE app, the Nix app, and then pooled it into two columns of an Excel spreadsheet. This was the easiest way to get all the data into one place for analysis.

I opted for edibles after reading several peer-reviewed articles that found that smoking in general can cause changes in heart rate. Edibles would remove that variable, as well as make it easy to consume a target dose. With edibles the math was simple—4 gummies contained 40 milligrams. I had some idea what I was getting into. A 2023 study in the journal Sports Medicine, looked at the effects of marijuana on runners jogging on a treadmill.

One of its findings was that weed could help athletes get a jump on tapping into the runner’s high. “It is possible that exogenous cannabinoids like THC or CBD might activate the endocannabinoid system in a way that mimics the runner’s high,” said Laurel Gibson, PhD, a researcher on the project. It was time for me to find out.

I wasn't "in Barstow on the edge of the desert when the drugs began to kick in," as Hunter S. Thompson wrote in Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas—I was in my basement getting ready to get back on the trainer. I queued up a chill electronic playlist to tap into the beats with my pedal stroke. I did the same 15-minute warmup I did prior to the first ride while I got all my sensors dialed in. Toward the end of my warmup I noticed something—I was getting sucked into the ride. If you’ve ever been on a trainer ride, then you know that the monotony of riding indoors can make you want to hit the eject button as soon as possible. On my first ride I was watching the clock to see when I’d be done, but on this warmup I quickly felt myself getting more hooked on my cadence.

Once the test ride started, I felt like I was more immersed in the virtual world compared to the baseline ride—I was the avatar. As I spun up and down hills, I focused on my breathing and cadence. I felt locked in, in a way that couldn’t have been more different from the first ride. I just wanted to keep going.

Even though it felt harder to push the same watts on this ride, I didn’t want to stop once the route was done. I had to remind myself that I was doing this as an experiment and it was time to get off the bike—I could have kept pedaling around that virtual world for hours. Again—not surprising. The Sports Medicine study found that marijuana increases enjoyment, enhances recovery, and heightens motivation during workouts. In these ways, at least, it seems marijuana’s effects on cyclists are similar to the runners in the study.

It turns out weed is not a performance-enhancing drug for me. Comparing the two rides showed there was a noticeable difference in heart rate as well as body temperature—two traditional indicators of performance. During the roughly 32-minute effort, my average heart rate went up 28 beats per minute (bpm) while my max internal body temperature went up almost a full degree after taking the 40mg dose. That suggests the THC and CBD in the gummies had a negative effect on my performance. While I wasn’t too surprised by this, I was surprised by what I felt versus what the numbers showed.

For an expert opinion, I shared my results with Angela D. Bryan, PhD, adjunct professor, Division of Medical Oncology at the University of Colorado School of Medicine, editor in chief of Annals of Behavioral Medicine, and a researcher on the 2023 Sports Medicine study. She quickly zeroed in on my 40mg dose and the rise in heart rate. “That’s a huge dose, actually, and THC itself causes an acute increase in heart rate. So that’s why you saw that,” she said. Her note on heart rate is important because if THC raises heart rate, that in and of itself can impact performance.

I didn’t have a drop in my ability to sustain power, and I didn’t notice an inability to recover when I tried to put in a dig on the climb. The biggest performance takeaway I had is this: THC and CBD can raise heart rate while riding, which can impact performance. But oddly, in the moment I didn’t feel that I was working harder or that my heart was pounding faster. This is a different and potentially positive effect of marijuana.

Not everyone is training for high performance—a lot of us just want to ride more. During my edible test I didn’t dread getting on the trainer, and once I was on it, I didn’t want to get off. I might have had a higher heart rate, but I enjoyed the experience significantly more. I could see this fitting in on trainer rides in general and zone one, recovery, or zone two rides more specifically. Of course, more research needs to be done on the long-term effects of THC and CBD on athletes.

This was just one trial, at a relatively high dosage. Overall, I found the experience pleasant, and the impact on performance modest—and the idea of experiencing the “runner’s high” sooner is appealing—especially on trainer rides.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#8946. How to Strengthen Your Arms and Wrists With Upward Plank Variations

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about Upward Plank Pose variations first appeared in the June 2007 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

What direction do you face when you practice yoga? Probably whichever way your usual practice space dictates. But the old yogis were very clear that we should face either east or north when practicing, per the classical yoga text the Gheranda Samhita 5.48. Why?

Yoga scholar Alain Danielou writes that the four cardinal and four intermediate points of the compass have special significance. The thunderbolt-wielding Indra, lord of all the protectors and prototype of courage and power in Hindu mythology, guards the east.

By facing in a certain direction when we practice, we acknowledge and draw on energetic properties for support and inspiration. So again, why east and north? East is the quarter of the rising sun, which Hindus revere as the “breath of creatures” or the source of all earthly life.

The sun represents the embodied Self, its dawn the emergence of the “light” of spiritual self-awareness and insight. North is the quarter of the pole star, called dhruva (pronounced DREW-vah) in Sanskrit, meaning “fixed, eternal.” Its constancy amid the ever-wheeling night sky is considered the embodiment of willpower, certainly a quality all serious yogis covet. In India too, north is the realm of the majestic Himalayas, where Hindu tradition places the mythic mountain Meru, thought of as the “navel” of the earth as well as the bridge to the celestial world of the gods and goddesses.

What compass directions would you assign to the back and front of your body? According to the yogis, your back body is the west, your front body the east. In Sanskrit, paschima means both “back” and “west,” while purva means both “front” and “east.” So this terminology gives us the names of two common and related poses: Paschimottanasana (Intense Stretch of the West Pose or, more commonly, Seated Forward Bend), which stretches your back body, and Purvottanasana (Intense Stretch of the East or Upward Plank Pose)—pictured here—a slight backbend and front-body stretch that provides a nice counterpose to its western opposite.

Purvottanasana stretches you all the way from your ankles through the thighs, groins, and belly, up to the shoulders and throat. It also strengthens your wrists and the muscles on the backs of the upper arms (triceps) and firms the buttocks—which, if you believe popular media claims, is a primary benefit of yoga. It will also help improve your sense of balance and calm. And it’s a great counterpose to the commonly practiced Chaturanga Dandasana (Four-Limbed Staff Pose).

If you have serious wrist, shoulder, or neck problems, practice this pose only under the guidance of an experienced teacher. You’ll need a chair, a block, and a wall to practice some of these preparatory poses.

Sit on the floor with your legs extended straight in front of you in Dandasana (Staff Pose). Rotate your thighs inward, big toes in, heels out, and press your palms to the floor slightly behind your buttocks with your fingers pointing forward toward your feet. If your shoulders protest, you can turn your fingers outward.

Bend your elbows and sink or hollow your front torso, spreading your scapulas as far away from your spine as possible. Rotate your upper arms inward and widen your elbows, letting the heads of your upper arm bones (humeri) jut forward. Enjoy the stretch between the scapulas for a minute or so.

Then straighten your elbows and lift your chest while leaving your lower body on the floor. Often, students simply squeeze their scapulas together and shove their lower front ribs forward, which hardens the front torso, restricting the free flow of breath, and compresses the low back. Instead, keep your scapulas wide and front torso soft.

Press the bases of your index fingers into the floor and hug your triceps against your humeri. As your elbows straighten out and your chest lifts, maintain the inward rotation of your upper arms, which will help the scapulas stay broad. Release your head back slightly, but don’t fully extend the neck. Trace the stretch along your front torso from your pubis to your sternum (breastbone).

Imagine directing your inhalations into the space behind your sternum (“imagine” because there’s no lung there, just your heart), increasing the lift of your chest. With each exhalation, reaffirm the opposing movements of the inner hands (down against the floor) and scapulas (up against your back). Hold for a minute or two. Repeat two or three times, until you feel confident you’ll be able to recreate the inward rotation of the thighs and arms and the actions of the hands and scapulas while maintaining the soft front torso when called on to do so in the more challenging circumstances of the full pose.

Next, sit on the front edge of a chair with your knees bent, heels directly below your knees. Wrap your hands around the back edge of the seat (for this first part of the exercise your upper arms will naturally rotate outward), thumbs pointing outward (Figure 1).

Inhale and slowly lift your buttocks away from the seat until your thighs, torso, and head form one long diagonal line, with your arms more or less perpendicular to the chair seat. Rotate your thighs slightly inward, and push (but don’t physically move) your knees away from your torso. The thigh rotation will tend to make your tailbone sag toward the floor, collapsing your belly, so firm your tailbone against your back pelvis and lengthen it. Hold this position for a minute, then sit back on the chair. On an inhalation, release the back edge of the seat and return to sitting upright. Take a few breaths.

If you like, repeat this exercise with your fingers turned forward, palms on the seat, and your upper arms rotated inward. Hold for one minute, release on an exhalation, and rest.

If you want to take this exercise to its limit, lift your buttocks again and extend your legs. Do your right leg first. Inhale and press out through your heel to straighten your knee, but suspend your foot a few inches off the floor. Then rotate your thigh inward, point your toes, and bring your sole to the floor. Just as the bases of your index forgers press the seat, so the base of your big toe presses on the floor. Repeat with the left leg. Once again, hold for a minute and release on an exhalation.

If you want to continue, brace the back legs of a chair against the wall and lay your block on the seat (if you’re using a wood block, cover the seat with a sticky mat to keep the block from sliding). Set the block on either its lowest or middle height near the front edge of the seat.

Sit on the floor right in front of the chair, knees bent, feet on the floor, heels 12 to 15 inches away from your buttocks, and lean back against the front edge of the seat. Press your hands on the floor with your fingers turned either forward, to the sides, or back—you choose—just in front of the feet of the chair legs.

Inhale and do what you did for the first part of the first exercise: Lift your thighs and torso parallel to the floor (heels below the knees), and then release your head back onto the block to take any pressure off your neck. If the block is too high or too low, come down and readjust. If you are having trouble opening your chest, it may help to reinforce the firmness of your palms against the floor, your scapulas against your back, and your triceps against the humeri. Then again, it may not.

Don’t get discouraged. Just practice this exercise every other day or so for the next few weeks, and you’ll be surprised how quickly things improve. Whatever happens, hold the pose for 30 seconds to a minute, then release to the floor on an exhalation. Smile.

If you can’t boost your chest, though, trying to extend your legs will probably make matters worse, so I don’t recommend it. But if your chest is reasonably lifted, then it’s acceptable to extend your legs.

Having trouble getting the balls of your feet, especially the bases of your big toes, on the floor? Position a rolled-up sticky mat on the floor where the balls of your feet will be when your legs are extended and press against that.

#8944. Can Your Road Bike Handle a Cyclocross Race?

A 33mm tire may fit, but mud clearance, gearing, and frame durability still matter.

A decade ago, it was still common to see Tour pros racing on 23mm tires, with 25mm considered progressive. Views on tire width have shifted. At this year’s Tour de France, most riders were on tires labeled 28mm to 30mm; mounted and inflated, many measured 30mm to 32.5mm. The widest setups measured in the paddock were more than 33mm—above the UCI cyclocross limit.

Road bikes with room for 32mm tires are increasingly common. Some clear rubber as wide as 40mm. So you might be wondering: Can I install a pair of 33mm cyclocross tires on my road bike and race the local ’cross?

As these photos show, I mounted 33mm cyclocross tires on Trek’s Madone 8 road bike. And there was even a bit of clearance, even though Trek states the Madone’s maximum tire clearance is 32mm.

But just because you can doesn’t mean you should. There’s more to racing cyclocross on a road bike than stuffing knobbies into any frame that clears them.

CX race bikes are designed to take a 33mm knobby tire with generous mud clearance. A road bike’s stated maximum tire width leaves room for some debris around a slick tread, but not for peanut-butter mud.

Then there is all the other stuff you will find on a cyclocross course: sand, ruts, off-camber turns, barriers, and sharp corners.

You’ll dismount, shoulder the bike, pound into bumps and holes, and crash.

Your road frame wasn’t built with all of cyclocross’s many charms in mind. The engineers I’ve asked about this point to the seatstays as particularly vulnerable to damage in cyclocross.

There is precedent, though. Toon Aerts won the 2025 European Cyclocross Championships on an Orbea Orca OMX road frame fitted with a fork from the Orbea Terra Race gravel bike. That’s a pro-level workaround for a sponsored athlete, not a green light for every road bike.

Your road bike’s gearing is probably too high for a ‘cross course, which is likely to feature steep, slippery climbs and slow technical sections. Road gearing can mean more dismounts; an easier gear can help keep you riding instead of getting off to push.

If you want to race ‘cross without buying a cyclocross bike, a gravel bike is a better place to start. It usually has lower gearing and is built for bigger impacts and rougher use. A gravel bike definitely has room for a 33mm tire. If it’s a modern model built for 50mm-plus tires, it’ll have heaps of mud clearance—so much that a 33mm CX tire might look a little lost in there.

And if you use your gravel bike, you can also use wider gravel tires. The UCI caps CX tire width at 33mm, but that only applies to races they sanction.

Your local CX series is probably not UCI-sanctioned.

Local rules vary, so check before you line up. If wider tires are allowed, a wider gravel tire may offer more comfort and grip—and could even be faster, depending on the course.

There’s a handling trade-off. CX bikes are made to whip through tight, slower-speed corners; gravel bikes usually favor stability. So a gravel bike might feel too long, too stable, and the steering too slow, on a tight ‘cross course. But you might actually prefer a more placid-handling gravel bike in the anaerobic blur of a cyclocross race.

So, can you ‘cross your road bike? Technically, yes—if a 33mm tire clears without rubbing, the course is dry, and your gearing suits the terrain. But just because you can doesn’t mean you should. If you already have a gravel bike, start there. Check the rules, fit the tires, and go have a race.

A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. Next up on his to-do list: a multi day bikepacking trip, and an e-bike race.

#8943. The Best Triathlon Suits of 2026, Tested by Real-World Triathletes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Best tri suits of 2026 rated and reviewed based on 10 criteria. (Photo: Triathlete)

Men's 2XU Light Speed React Sleeved Tri Suit

Women's 2XU Light Speed React Sleeved Tri Suit

When you look good, you feel good – and when you feel good, you race great. It’s no surprise, then, that when triathletes gear up for race day, they spend hours looking online for the best tri suit.

Indeed, in our 2025 Triathlete Community Survey, 88% of respondents said aesthetics were at least “somewhat” important, with 38% saying they wouldn’t wear what they felt was an “ugly” kit.

But a great triathlon suit is more than good-looking – ideally, it also needs to fit well, carry your nutrition stash, provide an aero- and hydro-dynamic advantage, and protect the tender bits from chafing.

We’re asking a lot of tri suits these days, but the industry has stepped up to the challenge. Legacy brands like Zoot and Coeur, as well as newcomers Ryzon and Tri-Fit, have made it possible for triathletes to find not only a suit that meets their practical race-day needs but also shows off their own personal style.

With so many options available, we asked the Philly Tri Club and Triathlete contributors to help with real-world testing of the top triathlon suits of 2026. The 150-strong club is all about creating an inclusive training community, and club members in a variety of shapes and sizes put tri suits through the paces, wearing them through workouts and races and making note of what works and what doesn’t in their triathlon kit reviews. Here’s what they had to say about the best triathlon suits of 2026.

In our 2025 Triathlete Community Survey, we asked readers what brands of triathlon apparel they had in their closets. Though more than 20 brands were represented, the top six are familiar names in the industry.

Pockets: 2 back pockets, 2 svelte front pockets, 1 neck ice pocket

The Regna Elite Trisuit offers a custom fit via an app that completes an AI-powered body scan for a fit based on your unique features. For the ultimate test, we tasked Triathlete contributor Jon Dorn and his wife Heather with testing it out. Jon stands at 6’6” and is self-described as very slender. His wife is 5’3” “buxom, and more powerfully built,” according to Jon.

“I’ve finally found a tri suit that doesn’t chafe my ass or distract me as various sensitive parts start smarting,” said Jon.

Heather noted that the suit was a 95% perfect fit, though the midsection was slightly loose. As someone who doesn’t fit into the “one-size-fits-most” size structure, she was still quite pleased. “This is the best my undercarriage has felt in a tri kit in years,” she reported after a four-hour training ride.

Ultimately, the pair found that the price tag is the biggest deterrent and only really justifiable if you’re someone who doesn’t fit into a standard tri kit well.

If you’re looking for a budget triathlon suit for a sprint or Olympic triathlon that won’t chafe, the 2XU Core Tri Suit is a safe bet. It lacks adequate padding and pockets sizable enough to carry enough nutrition for long-course training or racing, but at the $200 price point, it’s a rare find for short-course racing.

It’s light on compression if that’s your preference and when it comes to breathability, the suit was disappointing, so ideally plan to wear it in more forgiving weather, as our tester found that it trapped heat and sweat more than other comparable suits.

Our tester found it hard to criticize anything about this suit because it fit snugly and comfortably. While she doesn’t normally wear sleeved tri suits, she was pleasantly surprised by how thin and breathable the fabric on these sleeves was, to the point that she forgot the sleeves were even there.

The tri suit has ample compression, especially in the core. The one detractor is that this suit only comes in black or black and white, which is a little generic and not as fun as some of the other options on this list. User beware, too: our tester noticed a bit of color leaking when handwashing the suit. Consider wearing the suit for shorter training sessions or wearing a belt with additional fuel, as the two back pockets are medium-sized and diagonally aligned.

Pockets: 3 back pockets, 2 inner front pockets, 1 neck ice pocket

When it comes to tri suits, it’s the little details that make a brand stand out. In this case, Tri-Fit’s attention to pockets – six in total, including one explicitly for holding ice on your neck during hot races – is reason enough to consider the Vortex for a long-course race.

Testers liked the fit, fabric choice, design, pockets, and overall feel, noting that it looks great with small logos, lightweight fabric, and comfortable chamois padding for shorter events. The chest zips up tightly, preventing wind trap, and performed well during rides and runs.

However, there was substantial drag in the water, and the vent holes under the arms caused chafing – vented fabric would be preferable, as would slightly more compression on the legs. In all, however, the Tri Fit feels premium, and with a few minor design tweaks, could quickly become a favorite tri suit.

Pockets: 1 lower-back channel pocket, 1 neck ice pocket

This tri suit performed adequately in the heat, thanks to the use of smart temp technology, which dials up evaporation from the skin to the air as body temperature rises. The super-thin and light chamois also mitigates heat well, especially on long rides, and strategically-placed airflow channels on the shoulders and back help things feel cool and fast on the bike.

However, the top zipper rubbed against the chest, causing discomfort during running and biking. It also chafed at the neckline due to the lack of a zipper cover. Testers liked that it fit well, but disliked that the zipper needed a fabric cover and that the white top was see-through, especially when wet coming out of the swim or sweating on the run (women testers noted their sports bra was visible while wearing the suit in a race).

At $125, Black Bibs brand has created a budget-friendly triathlon suit that stands out in a market full of offerings $300 or more. But “budget” should not be conflated with “cheap” here – the suit fits well, provides exceptional compression, and is a classic style (men’s and women’s one-piece colorways include a solid black as well as a black bottom half with navy, burgundy, or white uppers). Openings for the legs and arms use silicone “power bands” to keep the suit secure throughout a workout or race, and no chafing was reported. The suit also proved extremely durable both on and off the race course, holding up through dozens of laundry cycles without shrinking, pilling, or splitting seams.

The initial impression of the chamois was mediocre, but improved with subsequent use and resolved itself after several rides. Testers reported drag when swimming, with the neckline sagging, and recommended use with a wetsuit. Dislikes included poor moisture wicking, especially in the upper body, and unusually high rear pockets.

Unlike some tri brands, where women’s suits are simply a smaller version of the men’s, Coeur tri suits are designed with a woman’s physique in mind, from the contours of the suit to the women’s specific seamless chamois. Testers also liked the supple fabric and one-piece design with a full front zipper and high-rise short beneath, allowing for breathability and extra roominess in the torso.

This tri suit performed exceptionally well on the swim and run, but some chafing was experienced on the bike – chamois cream is recommended. The arm openings run slightly small, so athletes with muscular arms should size up or opt for the sleeveless version. Luckily, Coeur offers a variety of competitively-priced women’s tri suit configurations in matching colorways: sleeved, sleeveless, sports bra/shorts, aero tops, and tri tops with built-in bras.

Testers liked the sleek, minimalist, and professional appearance of the monochromatic Arise tri suit, as well as its stretchy, comfortable, and “slippery” feel that allowed for movement and flexibility without chafing. It remained comfortable even when wet, ran true to size, didn’t create unnecessary drag, and worked well with other clothing. This tri suit generally performed well across all conditions and disciplines, with no reported poor performance or chafing.

However, a dime-sized hole appeared in the left armpit after two wears, which was surprising and disappointing, given the suit’s $335 price tag. Testers also wished the back pocket was deeper and had multiple compartments.

Pockets: 1 rear pocket, two side pockets, 3 interior pockets

Zoot has been a mainstay of triathlon apparel for more than 40 years, and for good reason – users recognize the balance of form and function present in many of its products. The suits, designed by endurance athletes, for endurance athletes, come in a variety of designs, including flashy patterns and colorways.

The latest offering from Zoot, the Ultra Tri P1, performed well during swims in the ocean, bike rides on a trainer and outside, and runs outside. Testers liked its comfortable and true-to-size fit as well as built-in UPF 35 sun protection fabric.

However, the pockets were not very big, making it difficult to carry proper nutrition during training rides or runs – testers recommended wearing the suit for short-course racing or long-course events only if nutrition on the course is plentiful. The zipper was also annoying and rubbed a bit, requiring multiple adjustments while running.

Overall, however, the suit was rated as “top-notch” for comfort, breathability, and weight.

Looking for more tri suit reviews? Check out our reviews of tri suits from Varlo, Swiss Side, Wyn, Synergy, and more in The Best Tri Suits for 2024.

## The Moment You Recline Into ANA "The Room" The flight attendant slides your suite door closed. You're somewhere over the Pacific, 35,000 feet above the ocean, enclosed in what ANA calls "The Room" — a fully private, floor-to-ceiling enclosed business class suite on a Boeing 777-300ER. The seat converts to a fully flat 78-inch bed. There's direct aisle access. The service is famously meticulous. And you're flying from New York to Tokyo in a product that rivals first class on most other carriers. This is not a fantasy. This is what 90,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles buys you on ANA's JFK → NRT route. ### The Math That Should Stop You Cold A one-way business class ticket on ANA between New York and Tokyo typically retails for **$6,000 to $12,000 in cash**. That's not a typo. Premium cabin trans-Pacific fares are genuinely that expensive, which is precisely why the ChooseFI community treats travel rewards as a core pillar of the FI lifestyle — you're unlocking experiences that would otherwise require years of extra saving. At 90,000 Virgin Atlantic miles for that same seat, your points are delivering **6.7 to 13.3 cents per point (CPP)** in value. To put that in context: most points are considered "good" redemptions at 1.5–2 CPP. This redemption is 4 to 9 times that benchmark. This is what a true sweet spot looks like. ### Why the Gap Exists Virgin Atlantic prices its ANA partner awards using a **fixed award chart** — a relic of the old loyalty program era when airlines published static pricing tables rather than dynamic, revenue-based pricing. ANA's own Mileage Club program charges 75,000–90,000 miles for the same route. Virgin Atlantic's chart prices it at 90,000, but — and here's the critical part — **with zero fuel surcharges on partner-operated flights**. What you see is what you pay. The result is one of the most compelling premium cabin redemptions in all of loyalty programs. The ChooseFI community's founding principle is that every dollar has a job. When 90,000 transferable points can do the job of $12,000 in cash, that's not just travel rewards — that's an asymmetric opportunity you'd be leaving on the table.

Here's the aha moment: Virgin Atlantic is selling you access to ANA's inventory at a price ANA itself doesn't offer domestically in the same way. That's the inefficiency. And it's hiding in plain sight.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club maintains a fixed award chart for partner flights. This is increasingly rare in a world where airlines have moved to dynamic, revenue-linked pricing. Because the chart is fixed, Virgin Atlantic charges 90,000 miles for ANA business class between North America and Japan — regardless of whether that seat would cost $6,000 or $12,000 in cash on the day you're flying.

When cash prices spike (holiday season, cherry blossom season, Golden Week), your points cost stays the same. That's not the case when you book directly through ANA Mileage Club, where pricing can vary, or through programs that have adopted dynamic pricing altogether.

This detail alone makes or breaks the redemption. Virgin Atlantic levies high fuel surcharges on its own metal (Virgin-operated flights). Book a Virgin Atlantic-operated long-haul in business class and you might pay $500–$800 in fees on top of your miles.

But when you book partner-operated flights through Virgin Atlantic — specifically ANA — those surcharges drop to zero. You pay government taxes only, typically $50–$100 on a trans-Pacific itinerary. That's it. No fuel surcharge games.

Here's a non-obvious but critical piece of tradecraft: you do not search for ANA award availability on Virgin Atlantic's website. Virgin Atlantic's search engine is limited for partner award space. Instead, you search on United.com, because United and ANA are both Star Alliance members and United shows ANA partner award availability accurately in its search results.

Find the space on United.com, confirm the flight numbers and dates, then call or use the online booking tool at flyingclub.virginatlantic.com to complete the booking.

Virgin Atlantic miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. This means as long as you earn or redeem even one mile every three years, your balance stays alive. Keep that in mind as you accumulate — a small card transaction through the program every couple of years is all it takes to protect a hard-earned balance.

Airlines partner with each other through alliances and bilateral agreements, allowing their frequent flyer programs to book seats on each other's flights. The pricing inefficiency occurs when Partner A prices Partner B's premium cabin at a different rate than Partner B charges through its own program. Virgin Atlantic maintains a fixed partner award chart that prices ANA business class at 90,000 miles regardless of demand or seasonality. ANA's own dynamic pricing can push award costs significantly higher during peak periods. This arbitrage between partner pricing and the operating airline's own program is the foundation of most airline travel rewards sweet spots.

This redemption is built for the couple or solo traveler who has been building a transferable points balance and is ready to make Japan the centerpiece of a bucket-list trip. If you've been diligently earning Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards and you want to experience what a truly premium long-haul flight feels like — without paying $8,000–$12,000 out of pocket — this is your redemption.

It's particularly well-suited to the FI-minded traveler who values experience over stuff. You're not flying business class because you can't manage without it.
