#8925. The Three Most Common and Costly Things People Miss When Buying a Used Bike

Before buying a secondhand bike, inspect these potentially costly trouble spots first.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

The customer came in right before a race because there was an issue with their shifting on the training ride. Yes, there was an issue with cable tension, but that wasn’t the biggest problem. The missing chip of carbon where the top tube met the seat tube overshadowed anything going on with the rear derailleur. When I asked the customer if he knew the chip was there, he said, “I bought the bike used and the seller said it was just a chip in the paint.”

Unfortunately, I’ve been on that end of the conversation with a lot of customers who brought in used bikes over the years. I get why someone would buy a used bike. Even when I ran shops, I would suggest used bikes as a way people could save money on a new (to them) bike. But there were too many times someone brought a used bike in for us to run through and we would find things like frame damage or wheels that needed to be replaced. Prices of new bikes have gone up dramatically over the last few years. Used bikes have their place for so many riders, but be aware of what you’re buying. Sometimes between the price of the used bike and then the parts and labor needed to make it ride-ready, you’ll be toeing the price of a new bike. Many of those new bikes also come with things like one free service or warranties from the manufacturer.

If you’re in the market for your next bike, it does make sense to consider used options. There are plenty of deals to be had on the used bike market. Here, I’ll give you the three most common mistakes I see people make when going the used route and give you my best practices when considering that used bike.

The biggest mistake I’ve seen people make is missing damage on the frame. I’ve had customers bring in used bikes where the frame had chips or cracks in the carbon or irreparable damage to aluminum frames. While there are shops that offer carbon repair, there are not a lot of reliable options for frame repair.

Let’s compare some pricing—an entry-level road bike is around $1,200 depending on the brand. Many times this will include some type of warranty, at least one free service or check on the bike, and at a minimum a free floor fit for you on the bike.

If the used bike’s frame needs to be replaced, then step one will be finding a frame compatible with as many existing components as possible. Many times parts like cables and housing, bottom brackets, and handlebar tape will need to be replaced when swapping to a new frame. Once a new frame is found, the parts listed above are added, and service gets put on the ticket, you are at or above the price of what that new bike would have cost.

This can be avoided by doing a thorough inspection of the frame when looking at a used bike. Do a thorough check of the frame—even the hard to get to parts like where the tires hide and under the frame. If I were buying a used bike I would bring a shop rag to wipe any dirty spots to do my due diligence. I wouldn’t recommend buying a damaged frame, unless you like it for wall art.

Wheels can be the second biggest money pit on a used road, gravel, or hybrid bike. When I was a service manager, we had to replace many wheels on newly purchased used bikes because the existing wheels were either damaged beyond repair or because the parts and labor to repair them outweighed the price of a new wheel.

The pricing was always surprising to people. Most shops I’ve worked in priced wheel builds around $100. If we were going to pull the hub (center of the wheel) and other components from the old wheel to install on a new wheel, there was a small, but additional charge. For people getting a used entry-level road, mountain, or hybrid bike, the labor of a wheel build, not including parts, could outprice the cost of a new wheel.

Reasons we would need to rebuild or replace a wheel were things like cracks in the rim at the spoke nipples, severe knocking in the hub (where the wheel develops too much lateral movement), or when the wheel was significantly out of true. Wheels can sometimes be straightened out (truing a wheel), but there are points where it can’t be brought back.

When looking at a used bike, there is a relatively easy way to check all of these wheel issues. First, look at the base of the spokes where they meet the rim. If you see cracks on the rim at any of these points, the wheel will need to get replaced. Once you check the base of the spokes, then hold the frame in one hand and the top of the wheel or tire in the other. Test for lateral movement in the wheel by holding the frame still and trying to move the wheel side-to-side. If it doesn’t move laterally, that’s another box checked.

Finally, spin the wheel while it is on the bike. Sometimes it can be hard to tell if the wheel is straight if the used bike has a flat tire. Try using your thumb as a guide. Hold your thumb a set distance from the rim surface (at least an inch). This technique will allow you to see if there is a severe wobble in the rim. Remember to keep your fingers far enough away from the wheel to not get them stuck in the spokes of the wheel as it spins. A small wobble can usually be fixed for under $50 at most shops.

This can be the hardest thing to see on a used bike because it can be really hard to tell how worn a drivetrain (chain, cassette or gears, and chainrings or crank) is with the naked eye. When someone is committed to buying a bike, a chain checker is one of the tools that can save you hundreds of dollars in the long run. A chain checker is a small, relatively inexpensive tool that checks how worn a chain is. By checking how worn a chain is, you can tell what other parts will need to be replaced. Many shops will recommend replacing an 11, 12, or 13 speed chain when a chain checker reads over 50 percent worn, replacing a chain and cassette or freewheel (gears on the back wheel) over 75 percent worn, and replacing chain, cassette or freewheel, and chainrings or crank (gears in the front near the pedals) over 100 percent worn.

If you don’t have the tool there are ways to check visually too. Sometimes you can see wear on the gears on the rear wheel (called the cassette or freewheel). When the teeth on the gears on the front or back start to become uneven and resemble shark teeth that is another quick visual check.

One fairly reliable trick to see if the chain is stretched is to try to pull the chain straight up and away from the gears by the pedals (called the chainrings). If it easily lifts up and away, and especially if there is a significant gap between the chain and chainring, there is likely a significant level of wear in the system. Having the chain checker is an easy way to tell just how much.

Pricing to get this fixed can easily exceed a few hundred dollars when all three components of the drivetrain (chain, cassette, and chainrings) need to be replaced. If the bike needs any additional labor that price can climb quicker than people expect.

When I ran a shop, I would always suggest customers get at a minimum a safety check or base-level tune-up on a used bike. This allows an experienced bicycle technician to inspect the bike, torque all the bolts and parts on the bike, and adjust things like shifting, brakes, and tire pressure. Even if the bike is a new bike that the seller said they just never rode, you never know who built it initially. I’ve had bikes in the stand that were in this category and the handlebar spun around with the slightest bit of pressure.

If you don’t want to take it to a shop, then consider options like local bike clubs, local bicycle nonprofits (our local example is the Coalition for Appropriate Transportation), or even an experienced cycling friend. Anyone who can run through the bike with an experienced set of eyes can help get you on the right path.

I used to suggest having the seller meet the potential buyer at my shop. This would allow both parties to be there when a service technician or adviser inspects the bike for an impartial assessment of the condition of the bike. Before using your local shop as the meet-up, give them a call to see if this is something they can offer.

This list includes the most common mistakes I would see specifically in the road, gravel, and hybrid categories of bikes. It does not touch on mountain bikes because that is an entire list in and of itself. Parts like suspension forks, rear shocks, dropper posts and pivot bearings are all things to be cautious about with used mountain bikes. If you have any other tips for buying a used bike let me know in the comments below.

Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#8924. I Wish Yoga Studios Would Stop Trying to Sell Me on Their Teacher Training Programs

Los Angeles-based yoga instructor Ramoni Overton questions whether a common trend across yoga studios is negatively affecting students. Overton is the creator of the YouTube channel Yoga With Ramoni.

I was brand new to yoga when I first experienced a teacher training sales pitch at the end of class. I had stood up after Savasana feeling pure bliss, practically floating off my mat. But suddenly the instructor was pedaling the studio’s upcoming yoga teacher training (YTT) to the entire room. I was surprised, but I mostly brushed it off, assuming it was a one-time thing.

But then it happened a second time. Then a third. And a fifth. After I heard the exact same sales pitch multiple times, my post-class high vanished before I even made it to the front door. It was replaced by a single thought. “Seriously? Again?”

This experience isn’t unique to me—it’s been happening to many other yoga students. And, in my opinion, it’s a reason why some of them might quietly not return to class.

As a yoga teacher for four years and a yoga student for nine, I’ve noticed that most students aren’t coming to yoga to build a second career. They already have full days and packed schedules. They’re coming to yoga to unwind, decompress, and experience a single hour in which the outside world completely disappears.

At the same time, I understand the reasons behind the post-class YTT pitch. Yoga studios have bills to pay, and YTT is one of the more reliable revenue streams in a business that runs on thin margins. But when studios push their instructors to pitch constantly (and when some instructors receive commission for every sign-up), the pressure is on. The yoga teacher who was supposed to hold space for you is now knowingly or unknowingly working a sales quota. That changes the energy of a studio, whether anyone admits it or not.

And it adds up to something that’s bigger than one annoying moment. Seemingly everywhere else in life, we are constantly being sold something. Ads interrupt us while we’re watching TV, listening to podcasts or the radio, and scrolling through social media. Yoga was supposed to be one of the few places that wasn’t also a marketing funnel.

Studios don’t need to stop sharing information about their YTT offerings. But they do need to stop treating every student on the mat as a sales lead. There are so many ways to share training info without disrupting the post-class quiet. A simple flyer at the front desk, an announcement on the studio schedule, or a free information session for those who are genuinely curious. Let people come, flow, and leave in peace.

If the training is enticing, students will ask about it on their own. You won’t have to sell them on it.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegantly simple once you see it, and understanding it will help you recognize similar opportunities across the loyalty landscape.

Most major airline programs have shifted to dynamic pricing — meaning award costs fluctuate with demand, just like cash prices. Alaska Mileage Plan has largely resisted this for its partner awards. JAL Business Class from North America is priced at a flat 60,000 Alaska miles one way, period. It doesn't matter if it's Golden Week in Japan or a random Tuesday in February. The chart price holds.

This creates an extraordinary opportunity because JAL cash fares are not fixed. They respond to demand, fuel costs, seasonality, and competitive dynamics. When those fares rise — as they have substantially in recent years — your 60,000 miles buy proportionally more value. The inefficiency widens the more expensive the cash fare becomes.

Here's a detail that separates Alaska from many other programs: Alaska Mileage Plan charges zero fuel surcharges on any partner award booking. This is significant. Some programs (looking at you, British Airways Avios) pass through carrier-imposed surcharges that can add $400–$800 to a theoretically cheap award. With Alaska, your out-of-pocket is taxes only — typically $50–$150 on a transpacific itinerary. Your 60,000-mile redemption costs you 60,000 miles plus roughly $100. Full stop.

Alaska Mileage Plan has no direct credit card transfer partners in the traditional Chase/Amex/Citi sense. This is the most important nuance of this redemption to understand. You cannot transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards directly to Alaska. Instead, the primary transfer path runs through Marriott Bonvoy.

The ratio is 3 Marriott points to 1 Alaska mile, and transfers typically take 1 to 5 days to complete. There's also the well-known Marriott bonus: transfer 60,000 Marriott points and receive 5,000 bonus miles, meaning 60,000 Marriott points nets you 25,000 Alaska miles. This makes earning Alaska miles via Marriott cards (like the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless or Brilliant) a viable — if not the most efficient — path.

Alaska allows a free stopover on one-way awards — a benefit almost no other major US program offers anymore. On a one-way award from the US to Japan, you could stop in Tokyo for several days, then continue to another destination, all for the same 60,000 miles. This is an advanced move that can double the value of a single award ticket.

#8921. Our Editors Rode Dozens of Electric Bikes. These 14 Are Worth Buying for Every Budget, From Under $1,000 to Premium

Find the right e-bike for your budget, riding style, and storage needs with expert-tested picks.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Fall is our favorite season for riding bike paths, rail trails, streets, and singletrack. Whether they’re commuting to work or school, running errands, or spending time with family and friends, more people than ever are choosing electric bikes for their rides. E-bikes make cycling easier, less sweaty, and more fun.

I’m a former product director for bike companies and a shop mechanic. I’m also a lifelong cyclist and ride dozens of electric bikes each year. I use them for everything from grocery runs to concerts and even going to the airport. This summer, I went almost entirely car-free thanks to an electric cargo bike.

Whether you’re picking your first electric bicycle, upgrading to a newer model, or adding another e-bike to your garage, dozens of great options are available—and our editors and staff have tested many of them. No matter your age, cycling ability, or budget, brands offer e-bikes that meet needs.

Tip for New Buyers: Don’t overpay for an electric bike, but spend what you can comfortably afford. If an e-bike is fun to ride, you’ll use it more often. It’s more cost-effective to buy an e-bike equipped the way you want it upfront than to upgrade it later. Also, remember: you cannot change an electric bike’s motor system if you decide you want more power.

The Aventon Level is our benchmark electric bike. It’s a great e-bike for commuting, running errands, or leisure riding. Over several years, the Level platform has proven to be reliable and low-maintenance. Plus, its price doesn’t break the bank.

Aventon split the 4th-generation Level into two models. The REC features a 750W hub motor with 80 Nm of torque. Aventon also added regenerative braking, increasing the bike’s range up to 75 miles. The pricier ADV edition features a mid-drive motor; it bumps up the torque to 100 Nm and range to 110 miles. Both versions come standard with fenders, a rear rack, lights, and suspension.

Another feature users will find quite useful is the Level’s connected features. The Level 4’s ACU (Aventon Control Unit) adds several smart features to the already well-equipped platform. The wheel lock and motion sensor alarm are passive theft deterrents when you stop for a mid-ride coffee or run into the post office. A 4G chip in the ACU enables GPS tracking in Aventon’s mobile app, so you can locate your bike if you forget where you locked it. 4G connectivity also allows you to set geofence restrictions on the bike for teens or housemates.

READ AVENTON LEVEL 4 REVIEWLEVEL 4 STEP-THROUGH

Plenty of commuter e-bikes cost far less than Specialized’s Turbo Vado SL 2, and they can probably do most of these things. So why spend twice as much as many popular options? I dive into the details in my story, “Stop Wasting Money on Cheap E-Bikes. Here’s Why Spending More Pays Off for Commuters.”

The TL;DR is: The Turbo Vado SL 2’s excellent ride geometry, silky-smooth motor, low weight, and premium components make riding fun. Together, these features make you want to ride the Vado every day and use it for more than simply getting to work. And thanks to Specialized’s extensive dealer network, you have somewhere to turn when it needs service.

This relatively affordable seven-speed model from Aventon delivers simplicity and style that is tough to beat. It’s even better than the original version, thanks to hydraulic disc brakes. A push of the throttle gets you started; then, the brushless hub motor gently assists your pedaling.

Along with disc brakes, the Soltera features integrated lights and turn signals, and the battery is hidden in the bike’s frame (rather than the bolt-on batteries found on many similarly-priced e-bikes). Best for smoother roads and bike paths, the Soltera delivers the essential features a city rider needs in a strikingly light 46-pound package.

Aventon also offers a singlespeed, Soltera 3 ADV with a Gates belt-drive system.

Tern’s cargo bikes are the gold standard for practical features, durability, and ride quality. This reputation makes the brand’s GSD (longtail) and HSD (short-tail) cargo models top picks for bike commuters, families, and riders looking to cut their dependence on automobiles.

The new third-generation HSD improves on its predecessor’s legacy. The HSD (short for “Haul Stuff Daily”) is a shrunken-down version of Tern’s GSD3 model released last year. The HSD3’s frame has a 419-pound carrying capacity (combined bike, rider, and cargo), added stiffness, and improved stability at speed compared to its predecessor. The P10e Sport configuration features the peppier Bosch Performance Line Sport motor and an electronic-shifting ten-speed TRP E.A.S.I. A10 drivetrain. The Sport motor’s 28mph assistance was a welcome upgrade for commuting and running errands alongside car traffic on local suburban streets. The 90 Nm of torque (15 Nm more than the standard Performance Line motor) also provides quicker acceleration from a dead stop and a little more oomph when loaded down with cargo or climbing hills.

While it’s the second-most affordable HSD3 model in Tern’s U.S. selection, the P10e Sport is certainly not a budget-priced e-bike. But for the extra cost over similar-sized cargo bikes, you get a proven and well-thought-out bicycle. The HSD’s features and design elements feel purposeful. A great example of this is the bike’s stowability: The HSD3 can be tilted and stored vertically, balanced on its rear rack. It also moves easily on its rear wheel when you need to park or store it. The handlebar and stem also fold down, making the HSD3 much easier to transport by car or SUV than almost any other e-bike.

For big city life, a simple bike that’s low-cost, easy to repair, and reliable usually beats out complicated designs. Lectric’s XP Lite2 is about as basic as it gets. It has a low-maintenance singlespeed drivetrain, a 300-watt hub motor, and a 375Wh battery. With its compact size, 20x2.5-inch tires, and twist-grip throttle, the XP Lite is perfect for zipping through traffic, commuting to the office, or heading to the gym or bar after work.

The XP Lite2 features only one gear and a 300W motor, so it’s not ideal for very hilly terrain. But with the throttle, you can get over small rises and bridges. Lectric also equips the bike with hydraulic disc brakes and front and rear lights. The XP Lite2 is also great for RVers and campgrounds, since it’s lightweight (about 48 pounds) and folds down to 36x16x27-inch dimensions.

It’s hard to beat the Portola Lite for the price. Ride1Up recently refreshed its mighty mini, and it has everything you need for quick commutes: power, speed, comfort, and portability. The Portola’s ride quality is premium, even though it costs thousands less than some high-end folding electric bikes. The bike is also solid: We’ve ridden the Portola for several hundred miles, and the only maintenance it has needed is air in the tires and chain lube. Runner’s World’s Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate has been testing the Portola for several months and notes, “It’s the perfect size for city commuting and doesn’t take up space in my garage when I’m not riding it.”

The updated Portola features a 750-watt motor with 90 Nm of torque; enough juice to ride even the steepest hills around town. Other changes over the previous generation model include integrated turn signals, dual-drive sensor pedal assist (cadence and torque), and Apple FindMy integration. The Portola Lite comes with a 100mm travel suspension fork, lights, and fenders. It also features upgraded hydraulic disc brakes—not found on every e-bike in this price range—which make stopping the 61-pound bike much safer.

Ride1Up offers the bike in four colors with two battery options. The 10aH (480Wh) internal battery gets up to 60 miles of range, but if you need more range or weigh over 200 pounds, opt for the 15aH (720Wh) battery for only $100 more.

Many “step-through” e-bikes don’t actually have a low step design. This makes it challenging for some riders to mount or dismount. However, the CTY e2.1, by REI’s Co-op house brand, has a fully step-through front triangle. The CTY is a great choice for older riders, those with reduced mobility, or others who seek an easy-to-ride e-bike.

REI equips the CTY e2.1 with a 250-watt hub-drive motor that provides smooth pedal-assistance up to 20 mph. It also features a suspension fork to smooth out bumps and potholes, an adjustable stem for a comfortable riding position, and hydraulic disc brakes for better stopping. For less than the cost of some e-bikes online, you can get a quality electric bike backed up by REI warranty and service.

The Current ADV is the priciest bike in this story, but for a good reason. Some electric bikes look a lot like mountain bikes, but that doesn’t mean they are built for real off-road use. Aventon’s new Current is the brand’s first full suspension E-MTB, and it is trail-ready right out of the box. Trevor Raab, Bicycling’s Senior Photographer and Test Team member, said, “The bike’s intuitive ride feel will please experienced mountain bikers and also benefit first-time mountain bikers.”

The Current ADV features an aluminum frame with 140mm rear wheel travel and a great-feeling motor with 750 peak Watts and 110 Nm of torque. (It also has a Boost mode that bumps power to 850W and 120 Nm of torque.) Rounding out the ADV are high-end components like a RockShox Psylo Gold fork, SRAM DB8 brakes, SRAM Eagle 70 Mechanical transmission, and a tubeless wheelset with Maxxis Minion EXO tires.

In his full review of the bike, “Aventon Goes Full Performance: The Current Electric Mountain Bike Is Surprisingly Dialed,” Raab particularly likes the Current’s easy-to-use interface. It’s loaded with ride data as well as the ability to tune the motor settings. If you don’t need rear suspension, check out Aventon’s updated Ramblas ADV hardtail E-MTB.

READ AVENTON CURRENT REVIEWMORE GREAT E-MTBs

Getting into E-MTB trail riding on a budget is tough. Low-priced electric mountain bikes often aren’t built strong enough for off-road riding (or weigh half a rider’s weight), and trail-capable models typically cost more than $4,000. That’s what makes the TrailRush a standout bike—for less than $2,000, you get a trail-ready hardtail you can take on singletrack and have some fun.

Ride1Up equips the 29-inch-wheeled TrailRush with a Brose mid-drive motor. With 90 Nm of torque, it isn’t as powerful as many new, higher-priced E-MTB motors, but it gets the job done. The TrailRush also comes stock with a dropper seatpost, four-piston disc brakes, and tubeless-compatible rims with Maxxis Minion tires.

Of course, to hit this great price, Ride1Up made some equipment sacrifices. The 504Wh battery isn’t as large as some peers (like the Aventon Ramblas), so you get less ride time between charges. Additionally, the 11-36T cassette and 38T chainring limit your ability to climb steep hills.

Compared to earlier iterations of the Aventure, the third-generation model has a smoother ride and feels more like a premium bike (without the high price tag). Aventon’s new torque sensor allows more control over the acceleration of Aventure’s 750W rear hub motor. Lighter-weight testers found earlier models had too much torque, but this Aventure remedied that fault. Additional features include a new head-unit interface, integrated turn signals, a front light, a rear rack, and fenders.

The Aventure 3 is an excellent fat-tire e-bike for commuters—especially on snowy days and gravel paths. Off-roading, it excels on doubletrack trails and cinder paths, but with this burly bike’s weight and components, it has limited functionality on singletrack and more aggressive mountain trails.

Aventon also offers the Aventure M, a mid-drive version of the Aventure. It keeps the same big, burly character but adds a more premium feel, a smoother, more powerful motor, and an upgraded drivetrain—along with a higher price. Those refinements cost about $1,000 more than the Aventure 3.

Buying an e-bike on Amazon can be a risky proposition, especially if you don’t know much about bikes or have much mechanical experience. However, sometimes you can find a good deal on a decent bike. At $500, the Heybike Cityscape isn’t the pinnacle of e-bike technology, but it will allow you to get out and enjoy some rides without breaking the bank.

I combed through dozens of Amazon listings comparing low-priced electric bikes, and this Heybike stood out for its combination of price and features. Then, I saw someone on the local bike path with one and asked them about the bike. The rider liked it and said it has been trouble-free (they noted a local bike shop assembled it for them). Heybike’s U.S. support line is available for warranty service or if you have product questions.

Don’t want to purchase from Amazon? Use this exclusive Bicycling discount link for $100 (applied at checkout) off the Cityscape 2.0, plus free shipping.

Many riders are attracted to the XPedition’s very appealing price. Currently priced at $1,399 for the single-battery model, it boasts an impressive 60-mile range and a top speed of 28 mph. (The dual-battery model for $1,799 doubles the range to 120 miles.) This makes the XPedition one of the most affordable electric cargo bikes around and a good option for riders seeking an excellent deal on an e-cargo bike.

“The XPedition’s capability surprised me”, said Test Editor Dan Chabanov. “Combined with the Lectric XL panniers ($150) and the Essentials package ($120), I comfortably carried several days of groceries for a family of three or one adult passenger.”

However, to reach a price like this, concessions have to be made somewhere. This results in a somewhat cheap feeling to the bike. Most of the XPedition’s parts are bottom-tier—with the notable exception of the brakes. The pedal-assist motor is powerful off the line, but at times, it feels erratic. The XPedition is adequate if you live in a very flat area or don’t need to carry kids or an adult passenger. Despite these faults, if you’re on a budget and looking to ditch the car for errands and trips around town, the XPedition is the cheapest e-cargo bike we recommend buying.

“Lightweight e-bike” might sound like an oxymoron to some, but a sub-40-pound weight is impressive when many electric bikes exceed 60 or 80 pounds. And often, e-bikes this light are pricey. Yet, the Velotric Tempo is only $1,499 and boasts a 39 lb. (claimed) weight.

Velotric achieves this weight reduction by ditching the bulky suspension fork (suspension forks on lower-priced bikes often don’t work all that well, to be frank), swapping heavy tires for 700x42c gravel tires, and using a smaller battery. Riders who need to carry the bike up any stairs or load it onto a bike rack will appreciate the reduced weight. However, heavier riders may want to test ride the Tempo before purchase, as lower-powered motors can bog down and reduce battery range for bigger-bodied people.

Many step-through electric bikes aren’t low enough for riders to easily get on or dismount. However, Heybike’s Venus features a very low-step frame that’s similar to designs used on city bikes. The Venus also has a 90-degree adjustable stem, so it’s comfortable to ride. At only 50 pounds, this e-bike is light enough for many riders to move around or carry up stairs if needed, and its 27.5” x 2.2” tires roll smoothly over pavement and crushed stone paths.

Bicycles are my life, and I’m a dedicated e-bike user and enthusiast. I’ve also worked in cycling for over 25 years. For the past five years, I’ve been riding and testing electric bikes, and I use e-bikes for my daily commute to the office. Before joining the Bicycling staff, I led product development for top bicycle brands.

Our editors test dozens of electric bikes across every cycling category, and we continually receive new models to evaluate. And our riding is for more than simply taking them on short spins; we use electric bikes in our daily lives. Commuting, school drop-offs, grocery runs, and daily transportation are only a few of the things we regularly do with e-bikes. We also hit the trails on E-MTB models to test their performance in real-world mountain biking conditions, not simply riding them around town.

In addition to ride-testing, our editors regularly talk to cyclists of all ages and abilities about their riding needs. This helps us craft our list of Best Electric Bikes: e-bikes that will meet your needs on the street, trails, and around the neighborhood. Two of the e-bikes in this story even made the final cut for our 2026 Bike Awards.

Electric bike prices range from entry-level models for less than $500 to premium machines costing almost as much as a good used car. However, our years of testing have proven that many of the best and most practical models live squarely in the middle.

We find that many standout e-bikes are priced between $1,500 and $3,000. These models strike a good balance between reliability and practicality, without requiring you to overspend on features or technology you don’t need. Electric bikes costing less than $1,000 often take shortcuts to achieve this, either by using lower-quality parts or offering limited service after the bike is purchased.

Of course, you can also spend much more on electric bikes. Premium e-bikes typically offer improved motor performance, higher-quality components, lower weight, or more tech features. However, for most general riding purposes, these bikes are overkill—but they‘re certainly fun!

→ Consider how much cargo you’ll need to carry if your riding involves commuting or running errands. Look for a bike with appropriate racks, mount points, and other accessories.

→ For singletrack and trail riding, look for mountain bikes with knobby tires, adjustable suspension, high-quality frames, and low weight.

→ Pay attention to weight. While fat tire e-bikes and cargo bikes offer versatility, many weigh over 90 pounds. If you’ll need to carry your bike up any stairs or lift it onto a bike rack, a lighter option will be a better fit.

→ Bike storage is another consideration. While most e-bikes don’t require excessive space compared to their non-pedal-assisted counterparts, ensure you have access to a power outlet where you plan to store it for easy charging.

Several e-bike brands, Aventon, Ride1Up, and Lectric, performed well in our ride testing and evaluations. These bikes might require some minor assembly at home, such as installing pedals, a seat, and tightening handlebars. We considered how easy bikes were to assemble in our recommendations. Many bike shops will not assemble or otherwise work on e-bikes they do not sell due to liability issues. The direct-to-consumer brands we recommend have dealers nationwide ready to support you.

Established bike companies, such as Specialized and Trek, manufacture e-bikes and have hundreds of dealers across North America. Additionally, REI sells its house-brand Co-op electric bikes (and models from Cannondale and Tern) in its stores.

There are three electric-assist classes available in the United States, and the use of each class of bike can vary by state, city, and area you are riding. Be sure to check local regulations before buying and before riding your bike.

Class 1: 20 mph max assist speed; throttle is not standard equipment.

Class 2: 20 mph max assist speed; throttle comes standard equipment.

Class 3: 28 mph max assist speed; throttle is not standard equipment

What this means: Class 1 motors kick in only when you pedal and stop helping you at 20 mph. Class 2 also offers pedal assist up to 20 mph, but these bikes can also have a throttle-powered mode that allows users to engage the motor without pedaling. Class 3 is pedal-assist like Class 1, but helps you until you reach 28 mph.

Other countries classify electric bikes differently, and many do not allow e-bikes to assist riders beyond 20 miles per hour.

Electric bikes generally feature one of two types of motors: mid-drive motors, which are contained in the frame at the bottom of the bike between the pedals; and rear hub motors, which are built into the rear wheel.

Bikes with rear hub motors are generally less expensive but are also less powerful. Mid-drive e-bikes tend to be more expensive, but are typically more reliable and higher performance. Because the extra weight on a mid-drive motor is centered in the bike and lower to the ground, these bikes are generally easier to handle than bikes with hub motors.

Measured in Newton meters (or Nm), torque is a rotational measurement of force—and the number to pay attention to when you want an idea of an e-bike motor’s output. More torque means more power off the line and more boost to your pedaling.

The heavier the bike, the more torque it needs. Lighter road bikes typically have 30 to 40 Nm of torque, and trail and cargo models (generally) have at least 80 Nm. Most commuter bikes fall somewhere in between.

The size of an e-bike’s battery is measured in watt-hours (or Wh). This measurement represents the energy stored in the battery and how many watts it can deliver each hour. The higher the number, the longer the range, but the faster you go, the faster you drain the battery.

So, if a 504Wh battery paired with a 500W motor gives you one hour of ride time at the highest assist, riding at about half that power will double your range.

Many e-bike brands seamlessly integrate batteries to make the bike look sleeker (and more like a traditional non-assist bike). Most batteries lock to the bike and come with a key that lets you unlock and remove it, which serves multiple purposes: You can remove the battery and charge it off the bike, plus a locked battery deters (and hopefully prevents) a thief from stealing it. An e-bike with the battery removed is safer for hauling on a bike rack and lighter for carrying up steps.

Since e-bikes can maintain higher speeds for longer than standard bikes, you want extra control when riding. Wider tires provide better traction and the freedom to leave the pavement with little penalty, and a suspension fork will help tame some of the rougher roads you might explore. Good disc brakes are a must, too, for slowing a heavy bike at high speed. This is not a place to skimp.

Some e-bikes have an integrated lighting system that turns on when you power up the bike. While this is a great feature, it’s not a deal-breaker if your bike doesn’t come equipped this way. It’s just as easy to attach your own since so many great bike lights are available.

E-bikes need regular maintenance and repair to stay in good working condition. Because they’re heavier and go faster than non-assist bicycles, e-bikes often require more regular service on parts like brakes, tires, and drivetrain components. We recommend having a good relationship with a local bike shop experienced in e-bike repair to keep your equipment running smoothly.

E-bikes use electronics for their motors, batteries, and displays. These parts are often proprietary to bike brands or even specific e-bike models, making replacement more difficult than parts on non-electric bicycles. Make sure to use the correct electronic replacement parts to avoid damaging your e-bike (or it catching fire).

Established brands usually (but not always) have a good supply of these parts for replacement, even for years after a bike goes out of production. Bosch and Shimano are two e-bike motor manufacturers with some of the most compatibility between bikes and stock parts for previous generations of systems.

Look for e-bikes from brands that offer at least a one-year warranty on electronic components (many brands’ warranties are longer) and make items like replacement batteries for your bike. These parts are usually not cheap (sometimes up to half the cost of a new bike), but it’s the difference between having an e-bike that can be repaired or becomes a bicycle-shaped paperweight if something goes wrong.

Following a dramatic increase in fires caused by the lithium-ion batteries used in electric bikes, there is a push from local officials, regulatory agencies, and advocacy groups across the U.S. for improved safety certification of e-bikes, batteries, and motor units. In September 2023, a New York City law took effect requiring that any e-bike sold in the city “has been certified by an accredited testing laboratory for compliance with Underwriters Laboratories (UL) standard 2849”.

However, just because something is marketed as UL 2849 compliant, tested to UL 2849, or even “certified to UL 2849” does not mean it is UL Safety Certified. Ibrahim Jilani, UL’s Global Director of Consumer Technology, notes: “Certification is always earned by a manufacturer and not a given when they undergo a product submittal. The UL Mark, or any authorized certification mark, can only be issued upon successful demonstration of meeting the requirements of the safety standard.” You can find UL’s updated list of products certified to UL 2849 here. You can cross-reference OSHA’s Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratories for a deep dive into the topic.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8919. Transform Your Core with This 10-Minute Exercise Ball Workout

An exercise (or stability) ball is an inexpensive but effective strength training tool for triathletes. (Photo: Getty Images)

For this article, retired pro triathlete and Triathlete contributor Emma-Kate Lidbury spoke to strength coach and former pro Dede Griesbauer about why this stability ball workout is so effective for triathletes.

Here’s the thing about strength training for triathletes: Almost nobody skips it because they don’t believe in it. They skip it because of the drive to the gym or the 90 minutes that don’t exist between that threshold bike workout and school pickup.

So what if we make life a little easier and remove some of the barriers to getting strength done?

This routine does exactly that and requires one piece of equipment – an exercise ball – and a patch of floor about the size of a yoga mat. No need for dumbbells, a bench, a gym membership, or the drive there. You can pick up an exercise ball for about the same price as a mid-range pair of goggles; it can fit into most any suitcase; and it might just help you find every stabilizer muscle you’ve quietly neglected since your last off-season strength block.

A stability ball is, by design, unstable. That’s the entire value proposition. It offers the following benefits:

Every exercise here demands you hold a neutral spine against something actively trying to move you out of it. Former pro triathlete turned strength coach Dede Griesbauer points out that this pays off in two places triathletes care about: run efficiency, and the ability to hold a stable position in the aerobars.

With an exercise like the rear foot elevated lunge (below), Griesbauer notes this forces each leg to work independently, which may reveal the left-right discrepancies a bilateral squat lets you hide. This matters for power balance on the bike and for not favoring one side on the run, which can help reduce injury risk.

Almost every movement in this routine trains multiple muscle groups at once. Griesbauer’s summary: It offers good “bang for the buck” with minimal equipment, minimal space, and minimal setup.

Griesbauer advises adding strength work to your hard days, not because it’s pleasant to stack lifting onto a threshold run, but because the alternative – sprinkling it across easy days – erodes the recovery that those days are designed to deliver.

“Make your hard days hard so that your easy days can be easy,” she says.

That’s the ideal. Griesbauer is also clear about what “ideal” might look like for an age-grouper with a job.

“Not everyone will have time to do their hard bike or run session AND make time for strength on the same day,” she says. “The good news is that this session isn’t heavy loading. These are good basic movements, so if you are time-crunched, adding them wherever you can is better than not doing them at all.”

Two sessions a week is the target, but once isn’t a failure. “Some is better than none,” Griesbauer says, “so if you can only do it once? Get it done once.”

Start with a single pass through all nine exercises (which should take approximately 10-12 minutes).

Once one round stops feeling like work, add a second. Then, if time allows, add a third. Three circuits should take you about 30-35 minutes and is plenty of stimulus for a routine that isn’t loading you heavily. Rest 30 to 60 seconds between exercises and a couple of minutes between rounds.

Progress through the workout in the order listed. It moves between lower body, core, and upper body so nothing fatigues to failure.

Stand on your right foot with your left leg extended behind you and the top of your left foot resting on the ball. Bend your right knee until your right thigh is parallel to the floor, keeping your torso upright and your weight on your heel. Now press your heel into the floor and return to the start position. Complete 10 repetitions and then repeat the exercise with your left leg.

Begin in a prone position with the tops of your feet resting on the ball, your palms on the floor underneath your shoulders, and your body forming a straight line. Now contract your stomach muscles, bend your knees, and roll the ball toward your chest. Pause briefly and roll the ball back until your body forms a straight line again. Complete 12 repetitions.

Assume a modified push-up position with your feet together, your body forming a perfectly straight line and your palms positioned slightly more than shoulder-width apart on the ball. Bend your elbows and smoothly lower your chest to within an inch of the ball. Immediately press back upward to the start position. If you have difficulty doing a full push-up, do a half push-up, bending your elbows only to 90 degrees before pressing upward. Complete 10 repetitions.

Start in a bridge position, face up, with your head and shoulders on the floor and your heels resting on top of the ball, your body suspended in a straight line between these points. Contract your hamstrings and roll the ball toward your butt. Pause briefly and extend your legs, rolling the ball back to the starting point. Don’t let your hips drop. Complete 12 repetitions. If this exercise is too easy, do a single-leg version, elevating one foot above the ball and pulling the ball toward your butt with the other leg.

Kneel on the floor facing the ball, lean forward slightly, and place your forearms on top of the ball. Pull your belly button toward your spine. Slowly roll the ball forward by extending your forearms out in front of you and allowing your body to tilt toward the floor. Concentrate on maintaining perfect alignment of your spine. Stop just before you’re forced to arch your back. Hold this position for a two-count and then return to the start position, exhaling as you do so. Complete 12 repetitions.

Lie facedown on the ball with your palms on the floor. Begin with the ball supporting your pelvic area. Now use your hands to drag your body forward over the ball until it is underneath the tops of your feet, keeping your body in a straight line. Pause briefly and roll back to the start position. Complete 10 repetitions.

Assume a modified push-up position with your palms on the floor, the tops of your feet resting on the ball, and your body in a perfectly straight line between them. Bend your elbows and lower your chest toward the floor. Go as far as you can without strain; it’s OK if it isn’t very far. Now press back to the start position. Complete 10 repetitions.

Lie face up with your upper back supported by the ball, your feet flat on the floor about 12 inches apart, your knees bent and your body forming a “tabletop” from knees to chest. Contract your calf muscles and raise your heels off the floor without allowing your hips to sag. Now lower your heels back to the floor. Complete 12 repetitions. If this exercise is too easy, do a single-leg version, first crossing your left ankle over your right knee and then doing the reverse.

Get into a plank position with your palms on the floor underneath your chest and the ball supporting your shins. Keeping your arms straight, press the heels of your palms into the floor and push your body backward so that the ball rolls up under your thighs. Go as far as you can and then pull your body in the opposite direction until you’re back in the start position. Complete 12 repetitions. If this exercise is too easy, start with the ball under the tops of your feet.

Instability is the point, which also means this routine isn’t universally appropriate. Griesbauer flags a few pointers worth knowing before you start. Note that none of these are a reason not to train. They just require you to adapt or swap movements if needed.

If you have a cranky lower back: The abdominal rollout generates high spinal extension and shear force if your core gives out mid-rep, which can be a genuine problem for anyone with disc history. The reverse crunch can pull you into loaded lumbar flexion if control slips, and a hamstring curl performed with dropped hips will arch and cramp the low back.

If you have “shoulder history”: Push-ups on a moving ball tax the rotator cuff hard, and the ball walk-out places prolonged, shifting load on the shoulder joint. Skip both if you’ve dealt with instability or impingement.

If you have wrist issues: The ball’s spherical surface forces the wrists into deep extension while the weight moves under you. Elevated push-ups shift more bodyweight forward onto the same joints.

If you have knees and hip flexor problems: The rear foot elevated lunge loads the front knee in deep flexion and stretches the trailing leg aggressively, which can be enough to tip the pelvis if your hip flexors are tight. Tight hip flexors will also hijack the reverse crunch from the lower abs.

If you have cramp-prone calves and hamstrings: The bridge heel raise fires the calves while the hamstrings are already shortened, which is a reliable spasm trigger. The hamstring curl frequently cramps athletes with weak hamstrings on the concentric.

If you have compromised balance: Any single-leg work raises fall risk. Have a wall or chair within reach if you feel you might need it.

#8918. VO2 Max Helps Riders Push Harder for Longer—4 Expert Recommended Tips To Improve this Key Metric

VO2 max isn’t just lab data—these training moves can improve how efficiently you use oxygen.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Sometimes it can feel like fitness for cycling is a spiderweb of data points leading to who knows where. Functional threshold power (FTP), resting heart rate, and watts per kilogram all get thrown around as the critical data point to show how strong a given rider is. However, one data point shows just how big your engine really is—VO2 max.

VO2 max is a measurement of the maximum (max) volume (V) of oxygen (O2) your body can take in and use exercise. It’s measured in milliliters of oxygen consumed in a minute per kilogram of body weight (mL/kg/min).

“It might help to think of your VO2 max like a car’s engine, but for your body,” Todd Buckingham, Ph.D., visiting professor of exercise science at Grand Valley State University previously told Bicycling. “The bigger your engine, the greater your capacity for being a good endurance athlete.”

If you want to add some horsepower to your engine you came to the right place. We have four tips from certified cycling coaches and researchers on how to grow your engine so you can elevate your cycling.

If you haven't incorporated high-intensity interval training (HIIT) into your training rotation yet, this may be the prompt to get you there: Research suggests that HIIT can significantly increase VO2 max compared to an endurance-only approach. For example, a study in Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise with 40 moderately trained participants found that HIIT boosted VO2 max better than running a long distance at a steady pace.

Another study, done with cyclists and published in PLoS One, noted that HIIT can increase VO2 max by up to 46 percent in six months, with participants doing HIIT sessions three times per week.

In terms of how to replicate these results in your own cycling, sprint intervals may get you there, especially if you focus on a longer recovery time. For example, a recent study in Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise looked at VO2 max in 14 participants who performed four 10-second sprints with 80 seconds of recovery compared to two 20-second sprints with 160 seconds of recovery. Gains in VO2 max were greater with the latter strategy.

How do you put this into practice? For a beginner or intermediate rider, a solid starting point is doing six work intervals for three minutes, with four minutes of rest in between, according to certified cycling coach Garret Seacat, C.S.C.S., of Train Absolute. He tells Bicycling this would look like:

“For a more advanced or experienced rider, you can typically handle a harder and longer time spent in that [max effort] zone with slightly less relative rest,” Seacat adds. “These are especially good for endurance and gravel racers.” Here’s what that entails:

Doing sprint intervals once or twice weekly can be a boon, but so can the type of long, slow distance riding that builds endurance, says certified cycling and running coach Paul Warloski of Simple Endurance Coaching.

“The long, slow distance helps build the metabolic adaptations, including increased mitochondria and capillarization, and greater fat utilization that leads to improved VO2 max because your body is more efficient at using oxygen,” he tells Bicycling. “An example of this pace is doing a several-hour ride where you are easily able to talk with someone.”

Research in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health looking at VO2 max in endurance athletes backs this up, and also adds that as you increase performance level through endurance training, the more stable your VO2 max can become over time.

While cycling intervals are helpful for VO2 max, research indicates that strength training can play a role as well. A meta-analysis in Sports Medicine looked at training variables for runners, researchers looked at the effects of high-load strength sessions (heavier weights with a lower number of reps), plyometric training, isometric training, and submaximal load sessions (involving more reps with lighter weights).

They found high loads improved running economy—a terms that refers to using oxygen efficiently, similar to VO2 max—the most, and those results would likely apply to cycling, according to principal author Cristian Llanos-Lagos, Ph.D., researcher in sports sciences at Universidad Pablo de Olavide in Spain, and certified cycling coach. That’s because this type of training created neuromuscular adaptations that boosted recruitment of lower-body muscles, he tells Bicycling.

“All strength training provides benefits, and we do believe it’s important to include multiple types because they can offer different advantages,” he says. But when it comes to increasing VO2 max specifically, throwing some high-weights, low-reps sessions into your training mix may yield some efficiency gains.

Like any training plan that focuses on progress, the key is consistency, suggests Warloski.

To keep riding regularly, create a plan, especially if you’re aiming for more interval workouts. For example, if you start with one HIIT workout per week, add in another weekly session on a non-consecutive day after about four weeks. Focusing on that type of progression from the start can help you create a training framework that leads to VO2 max gains.

Also, check in on your perceived rate of exertion if you’re not doing VO2 max assessments on a regular basis. When your sprint intervals or endurance rides begin to feel easier, that’s when it’s time to add more challenge as a way to keep progressing. (But also celebrate those wins of efforts feeling easier—that means your increasing your VO2 max.)

Over time, it’s likely that even without knowing your specific VO2 max number, you'll start to build cycling economy in a meaningful way.

Elizabeth Millard is a freelance writer focusing on health, wellness, fitness, and food.

#8917. 4 Things You’re Doing in Yoga That Might Worsen Lower Back Discomfort

Monica Bright is a yoga teacher whose continuing education centered on injury mechanics and movement. She breaks down the common yoga mistakes that could be worsening lower back discomfort, and offers options for relief. You can also learn more about yoga poses for your lower back.

Lower back discomfort is one of the most common pain points among people worldwide. If you fall into that category and also do yoga, chances are you’ve expected the practice to bring you relief. But certain movements in yoga, and how you approach them, can sometimes have the opposite effect of the lower back release that you were hoping to achieve.

Learning to recognize what triggers tightness in your lower back can help you make more supportive choices on and off the mat. That way, you’re still working toward undoing your discomfort, but without accidentally worsening it.

Whether you’re in class or at home, or even moving throughout your everyday life, notice whether any of the following approaches to movement worsens your lower back sensitivity—and explore the following alternatives that might help relieve your discomfort.

Some people’s lower back strain is aggravated by moving too quickly. This is often the case with forward rounding. Think Seated Forward Bend or reaching down to pick something up off the floor. Moving slowly allows you to pay attention to the sensations in your body and ensures you’re not accidentally forcing yourself to move too far into a stretch and tweak your lower back.

What to try instead: Throughout your yoga practice, and even during your day, ask yourself, “How does it feel when I move more slowly?”

The “neutral” position of your spine that you commonly hear yoga teachers mention includes several curves, including one in the lumbar spine that is concave, meaning it curves inward. But many students have a tendency to round the lower back during certain poses, such as forward bends and Chair Pose, which can have the effect of flattening the lower spine and causing tension.

What to try instead: Maintaining that neutral spine can be more beneficial than “flattening” it for some students with a track record of stiffness and soreness in the lower back. That comes into play in several common yoga poses.

In Chair Pose, for instance, there is a tendency to draw the core toward the spine so much that it counteracts the natural curve in the lower back. Maintaining a neutral spine means keeping the length in your lower back rather than tucking the tailbone.

In Standing Forward Bend, keeping a neutral spine means being aware if you are rounding your lower back as you reach forward and, instead, hinging at your hips, perhaps bending your knees, and not being concerned with how far forward you fold.

However, some students find a greater sense of ease in the lower back by rounding forward. Ask yourself, “Does my lower back feel better, or worse, with rounded forward folds?”

If your lower back is sensitive, your yoga practice might look different from the person’s on the mat next to you—and that’s okay. The goal in yoga isn’t to push past discomfort, but to find the alignment in which your lower back feels good. And sometimes that means taking variations.

What to try instead: Explore variations of poses—some of which might include using props, such as blocks—to help support your movements. Take Happy Baby, for example. Drawing your knees toward your chest and holding the backs of your thighs might feel more supportive to some. When sitting in a forward bend, placing a blanket underneath the lowest part of your back to slightly elevate your hips and provide more room for your lower back might be your preferred version. Finding the movement options that feel tolerable for you can be enormously helpful while you’re learning to prioritize your lower back.

Stress, poor sleep, a sense of being overwhelmed, even anxiety surrounding practicing certain movements can put your body on high alert and cause your nervous system to brace for impact. This has the potential to turn up the volume on physical discomfort. Understanding how to downregulate your nervous system, on the other hand, can help your entire body relax.

What to try instead: You’re likely familiar with some of the practices that activate your parasympathetic nervous system, including resting in poses such as Child’s Pose, Legs Up the Wall, or Crocodile and practicing various pranayama (breathwork) techniques, including Box Breathing or simply lengthening your exhalations. Even slowing the pace of your practice and taking the variations that feel good to you are ways of signaling to your nervous system that you’re safe. Experiment with one or two calming exercises prior to your next yoga class or at-home practice.

Practicing with these ideas in mind will ultimately help you recognize how to support your body when practicing yoga. This doesn’t mean you need to have to have all of the answers. It simply, but it does means that you are present, aware, and listening to your own body’s signals.

#8913. Post-Race Weight Gain: Why You’re Heavier After Finishing a Race (And Why It’s a Good Thing)

You wake up feeling sore and puffy the day after a race, step on the scale, and confirm what you intuitively feel: you’re a few pounds above your pre-race weight.

But why? Logically, a massive calorie burn (up to 10,000+ calories for an Ironman!) should tip the scale the other way, so something must be wrong.

Your first impulse may be to cut calories or jump right back into training. Please don’t! What you’re seeing is your body’s normal physiological response as it goes into full recovery mode.

Post-race weight gain isn’t the same as the off-season weight drift many athletes experience. That weight tends to build over months and is a separate conversation about energy balance. The jump you see on the scale in the first 24 to 72 hours after the race is mostly water. Specifically, your body is hard at work replenishing glycogen, rebuilding plasma volume, and retaining water and sodium as part of its hormonal stress-and-repair response. It’s most noticeable after a half or full iron-distance triathlon, where fueling, fluid intake, and stress load are highest.

Let’s dig into what’s going on, and why this temporary bump is actually a good sign.

Long-course races drain your muscle glycogen. As long as you eat plenty of carbs, your body starts refilling those stores within the first few hours after you finish. But the longer the race, the more muscle damage, which slows the process.

After a long-course race, full restoration can take several days, rather than the roughly 24 hours we see after shorter events. Here’s the kicker: each gram of newly synthesized glycogen is stored with approximately three grams of water. So, replenishing 400–500 grams of muscle glycogen adds about 3.5–4.5 pounds, mostly from water, packed in your muscles. In other words, much of the bump you see on the scale in the first few days is restored fuel.

Glycogen isn’t the only reason the scale climbs. It’s normal to finish a long race dehydrated, since even a solid race hydration strategy can’t fully offset hours of sweat losses. In the 24 to 72 hours after the race, fluid-conserving hormones (aldosterone and vasopressin) remain elevated, signaling your body to hold onto fluid to restore plasma volume and electrolyte balance. The extra water weight won’t stick around long, so don’t cut back on fluids or salt to bring the number down. Your body needs both right now.

Racing 70.3 or 140.6 miles puts your body under more stress than a typical training day. During and after the race, cortisol, your primary stress hormone, spikes, signaling your body to retain water. Prolonged physical exertion causes muscle microdamage and inflammation.

The longer, hotter, and tougher the race, the longer recovery may take. As your body begins repairs, fluid moves into damaged tissues, which can explain your tight, swollen legs. You’ll notice improvement when your kidneys start clearing the excess fluid, leading to more frequent bathroom visits. A little puffiness for a couple of days post-race means the repair process is underway.

As training volume comes down after a race, you might expect your appetite to follow. And, for the first several hours, it often does, since hard effort can temporarily suppress hunger. But over the next day or two, it returns with a vengeance. That’s because a slower-moving hormonal system (primarily ghrelin and leptin) signals your brain to respond to the energy deficit you built up on race day.

You may feel hungrier for several days, often craving energy-dense, salty, carb-rich foods (think fries, burgers, and pizza). And all that yummy food, along with the water and sodium that come with it, adds to the scale number too. It’s not a lack of willpower or a total loss of control; it’s your body refueling.

Following an endurance race, some swelling is expected, but I’d be remiss not to flag a few scenarios that, although rare, require medical attention.

If one leg swells, especially with calf pain, warmth, or redness, it may indicate a blood clot. Swelling with shortness of breath or chest pain is an emergency; seek immediate attention.

Dark cola-colored urine with severe muscle pain or weakness could signal rhabdomyolysis: a condition involving severe muscle breakdown that can lead to kidney damage.

And if you finish the race heavier than you started and experience confusion, headache, or nausea, it could be hyponatremia (low blood sodium); seek medical help right away.

For most athletes, a few extra pounds in the days after a long-distance race signals a healthy recovery. Still, it can be tempting, especially if you keep close tabs on your weight, to see the number go up and immediately want to cut back or restrict.

Resist the urge. Your body needs carbohydrates and protein to rebuild glycogen and repair tissue; your fluid and electrolyte balance needs restoring, and your immune system needs adequate energy while under duress. Restricting food and fluids now won’t get your weight back on track. It will delay glycogen restoration, prolong fatigue and soreness, and potentially increase your risk of illness.

As your fluid levels normalize and inflammation subsides, most of the extra weight comes off naturally, typically within three to seven days. You’ve demanded a lot from your body in training and on race day, so give it what it needs: plenty of nutrient-rich food, adequate hydration, rest, and quality sleep. Then step back and trust your body and the process.
