#8870. Cold, Dark, Rainy? The 10 Best Editor-Tested Indoor Bike Trainers Keep Your Training on Track

Our editors tested the best indoor bike trainers for winter miles, Zwift rides, and every budget.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Well, friends, it’s that time of year again. Colder temperatures and shorter daylight hours mean indoor riding season is right around the corner for many of us—if it hasn’t already arrived where you live. But thankfully, newer trainer tech and digital connectivity make those boring nights spent staring at your basement wall or garage door while endlessly spinning the pedals a thing of the past.

Smart trainers—some priced under $500—connect to Zwift and Rouvy, popular platforms that feature virtual worlds, group rides, and even organized races. Plus, lower prices on nicely-equipped indoor bikes mean you no longer have to wrestle with putting your bike on the trainer or ruining pricey components with sweat.

Our editors test trainers year-round, from budget-friendly units to the most advanced smart bike models currently available. We do workouts and ride a ton of base miles; some staff even compete at a high level in virtual racing leagues, giving us important feedback on trainer accuracy, stability, and durability.

The Wahoo Kickr Core 2 with Zwift Cog and Click is our Best Overall Indoor Trainer because it’s the perfect choice for most riders. It combines Wahoo’s excellent base-model direct-drive trainer with Zwift’s singlespeed cog and virtual shifting. The system sets up easily and works with almost any bike, regardless of gear range or number of speeds. (You can easily swap the Zwift Cog with a cassette if you don’t like the virtual gearing.) This enables multiple riders in a household to share one trainer, even if their bikes have different drivetrains or gearing.

I used the first-generation Kickr Core as my home setup for four years without any issues. Wahoo’s recent updates to the Core only make an already great smart trainer even better. Test Editor Dan Chabanov recently used the new Kickr Core 2 for three months after switching from the more expensive Kickr V6. He said, “Honestly, I can’t say I’ve noticed any kind of downgrade.”

On paper, the Kickr Core 2 has lower maximum wattage, less grade simulation, and slightly less claimed accuracy. In practice, the ride feel is almost identical on both models. Like the Kickr V6, the Core now features Wi-Fi (along with Bluetooth and ANT+) for smooth connectivity and faster data transmission for online events. “Truly, the only reason to opt for the pricier V6 is that it folds slightly smaller and is easier to move around,” Chabanov concluded.

The Zwift Cog uses virtual shifting to change gears instead of your bike’s shifters and derailleurs. Unfortunately, virtual shifting only works in Zwift. If you plan to ride without Zwift (or on another platform), purchase the Kickr Core 2 with a cassette.

Tired of putting your bike on the trainer every time you want to ride indoors?

Dedicated training bikes, such as the Zwift Ride, are a great option for indoor riding. This way, you have a bike on the trainer that’s always ready to ride. No more fumbling to remove your wheel or wearing down tires. The Ride’s adjustment range also makes it easy to set up and share with multiple riders in a household.

“After more than a year of heavy use by my wife and me, the Zwift Ride has proven to be a durable, impressively quiet alternative to abusing our 'good' bikes on a trainer, with excellent Zwift integration and easy adjustability for our multi-rider household,” said Senior Test Editor Matt Phillips.

Zwift’s recent updates addressed our criticisms of the original Ride. The V2 now fits more riders (4’10” to 6’6”), adds saddle adjustability, and increases the bar diameter. It also includes Zwift’s multi-position crank with lengths from 160mm to 175mm, which used to be a $100 upcharge.

If you ride indoors and want a dedicated setup that integrates with Zwift out of the box (and don’t want to spend thousands of dollars for a premium indoor bike), the Zwift Ride is an excellent option. Zwift sells the Ride Smart Frame alone (without a trainer) for $800 if you already have a direct-drive trainer.

Since launching in 2012, the Wahoo Kickr has consistently been one of the best indoor trainers and a favorite of Bicycling’s staff. While the sixth version of the venerable smart trainer is more of an update than a wholesale redesign, the changes help the Kickr rank ahead of other high-performance smart trainers.

The latest iteration features the same flywheel as the previous one, so the two units look virtually identical. As a result, both generations experience the same ride feel. The Kickr ramps up smoothly and correctly as you accelerate. Power accuracy is very good, and most riders will find the claimed 1-percent accuracy to be true.

Despite its high price and lack of cassette-sizing options, the latest Kickr is a solid choice. It’s the best option for performance-minded cyclists who push big watts or racers who require accuracy and improved connectivity for online events.

If you need a basic, budget-friendly trainer that gets the job done in a pinch—and offers compatibility with third-party apps like Zwift—the Tacx Boost Trainer Bundle is a solid option. With its magnetic roller, you can manually adjust resistance across ten levels. And because the Boost uses magnetic resistance instead of fluid or fans, it stays relatively quiet. The loudest sounds you’ll hear are your drivetrain and the tire on the roller.

The bundle includes a Garmin speed sensor and a front wheel block to keep your bike level while riding. It also folds up easily for compact storage. For an easy-to-use, low-cost, no-frills setup, this one covers the essentials.

The Saris Fluid2 is a good trainer at a reasonable price. This makes it a solid pick for riders who need something basic to keep up with their training plan on rainy days, rehab from injury, or get back into riding before heading outside onto the bike path, road, or trails.

The Fluid2’s wheel-on design means you don’t need to fumble with your drivetrain to set it up, and the fluid resistance provides a smooth, progressive ride feel. Although this version isn’t compatible with Zwift, Rouvy, or other online platforms, the Saris combo kit (for $40 more) includes a wheel sensor that adds connectivity. Also be sure to get an adaptor kit if your bike has a thru axle rear wheel.

Instead of buying that no-name $50 or $80 trainer, spend a little more for a proven trainer from a trusted brand. While it looks similar to Saris’ Fluid 2 (above), the Mag Plus uses a magnetic sensor to provide resistance instead of fluid. This saves a little money and gives you a linear feel (versus the Fluid’s progressive resistance). However, a big downside is that they tend to wear out tires pretty quickly, especially pricey, high-performance rubber.

Mag trainers have been around for decades (I’ve had several from different brands over the years); the tech hasn’t changed much and they don’t have any smart features. If you plan to ride Zwift or Rouvy, you need to install a wheel sensor. If you need a super basic trainer that gets the job done for only $100, the Mag Plus is your best bet.

The Neo 3M matches the Wahoo Kickr in power measurement (up to 2,200 watts with 1% accuracy) and maximum simulated gradient (up to 25%), but it has two unique features. The Neo generates its own electricity, so you can use it without external power (though it works best when plugged in). And, like an old-school Nintendo Rumble Pack, the Neo 3M vibrates to simulate a wide range of road surfaces—from gravel to cobblestones to concrete slab roads—when you’re riding Zwift.

Unlike other direct-drive trainers that use belts or rollers to transmit power, the Neo 3M uses a metal flywheel with magnets that interact with electrical coils to moderate resistance. Combined with the built-in motion plates, the trainer has an impressively realistic ride feel. However, the Neo 3M lacks a native high-speed data transfer mode or built-in Wi-Fi—a great feature for competitive virtual racing—but Garmin offers a separate adaptor.

The Wahoo Kickr Bike Pro is the indoor trainer of choice for riders seeking the best possible experience—and who have the space for a dedicated setup. At $4,000, it’s like investing in an extra bike that you can’t even ride outside. However, for many riders, the price is worth it since it’s always ready to go. You don’t need to install a bike or connect any devices. Plus, highly corrosive sweat and salt from trainer rides won’t damage your outside bike.

The Kickr Bike Pro adjusts to almost all bike fit measurements. Or, if you had a Guru, Retül, or Trek bike fit, you can plug the dimensions into the Wahoo app for more precise setup. Since the Bike uses virtual shifting, you can program it to any Shimano, SRAM, or Campagnolo drivetrain you want to ride. You can select the gear ratios and the number of teeth per cog.

The Kickr Bike Pro’s incredible ride feel comes from its high-tech flywheel with motor; it adds resistance while simulating the inertia of real-world riding. The Pro provides a coasting feel along with realistic braking and shifting. The system also features a piston-like mechanism that reflects virtual elevation changes by adjusting the angle between the bike and the ground (up to 20% incline and 15% decline).

If the Kickr Bike Pro’s $4,000 price tag is a little out of reach, check out the Kickr Bike Shift. It’s similar to the Pro in adjustment, but ditched the fancy flywheel and gradient-change feature—and it saves you almost $1,500.

Feedback’s Omnium Over-Drive is compact, lightweight (14 pounds), and sets up and breaks down fast. That’s why these portable trainers are ubiquitous in parking lots and team tents at bike races. These same traits also make it a great option for riders with small apartments or training while away from home.

However, this portable trainer isn’t light on features. Two 4-inch magnetic drums provide progressive resistance up to 1,050 watts (at 55 mph). Thanks to its height-adjustable fork mount and sliding base, the Over-Drive accommodates most bikes, wheel sizes, and quick-release or thru-axle configurations. Feedback includes a durable tote bag for storage under a bed, in your garage, or in a car trunk.

The trainer’s compact size makes it easy to carry on a plane as checked luggage (or in your bike bag)—I brought it along many times on trips to Asia and Europe. Plus, the Omnium’s quiet ride won’t disturb neighbors in a hotel room.

Wahoo’s unique-looking Kickr Rollr is a novel approach to indoor trainers. It’s a great option for those who need to install or remove their bike quickly. This makes it easy to use in a pinch, such as when an afternoon thunderstorm rolls in and threatens to cancel your training ride.

At the front, the Rollr features an A-shaped bracket that holds your bike’s front wheel with a tool-free clamp that accommodates tires up to 2.1 inches/53mm wide. At the back, the Rollr’s two drums cradle your bike’s rear tire, and an external flywheel adds resistance.

This design makes it quick and easy to put a bike on the Kickr Rollr, swap out multiple bikes, or share a trainer with other riders. However, we don’t recommend this trainer for riders who do a lot of out-of-the-saddle, high-intensity training or for users who regularly race on Zwift. (A direct-drive trainer will be better suited for these tasks.)

While the Rollr is adjustable for different wheelbases, the adjustment is limited and optimized for road bikes. This means long-wheelbase mountain bikes might not fit (most road or gravel bikes shouldn’t have any issues). Since the trainer doesn’t read power, you must have a power meter to use the Rollr’s smart features.

Direct-drivetrainers attach to your bike’s rear dropouts and replace your rear wheel with a resistance unit. These trainers are typically quieter than other systems, provide more accurate power readings, and are ideal for high-power efforts.

Friction trainers use a roller pressed against your bike’s rear tire. They’re lighter, (usually) more affordable, and more portable than other systems. However, friction trainers can be very noisy and wear out tires.

Rollers are a time-tested indoor riding platform. They use three drums (rollers) that you ride on, so they require balance. While some rollers have resistance, many don’t.

Smart bikes are dedicated indoor training bikes. These trainers are heavy and take up space, but they’re a great option if you have a bigger budget, are tired of taking your bike on/off the trainer, or don’t want to wreck your outdoor bike with sweat and salt.

Typically, a smart trainer is an indoor trainer that can wirelessly communicate power data with a training app on a smartphone or computer. Most smart trainers also work with virtual riding platforms like Zwift by automatically adjusting resistance to simulate changes in terrain.

The popularity of online riding platforms means most newer trainers are “smart” and will both transmit your data and adjust resistance. These features often add to the cost of a new trainer. But prices are falling; you can find connected trainers—such as the Saris M2—for less than $200.

If you want to try Zwift but don’t have a smart trainer, you can still log virtual miles using a Bluetooth speed sensor. Check out our guide to getting started here.

Compatibility: With axle attachment standards and widths frequently changing, check if the trainer you want offers different attachment options (such as thru-axle adaptors, or for direct-attachment trainers, free-hub options). Some trainers come with them. If yours doesn’t, you’ll need to purchase them separately. The Robert Axle Project is my go-to resource for replacement thru-axles and adapters.

Noise: While most manufacturers can get away with using words like “silent” and “virtually silent” to describe the noise level of their trainers, there are other factors to consider, such as the sound your bike’s drivetrain makes as you pedal, and if you use one, the fan that’s whirring away to keep you cool and simulate wind speeds. To get a better idea of how loud “silent” actually is, we used a decibel meter to record the noise levels of each trainer being ridden at 15 and 25 mph. Decibels ranged from 68 (comparable to a vacuum cleaner) to 85 (a diesel truck going 40 mph); the fan alone measured 71. To get an idea of how significant a seemingly minor jump in decibels can be, 70 is twice as loud as 60, and 80 is twice as loud as 70.‌

Stability: Trainer crashes are rare, but not unheard of when you’re going cross-eyed trying to beat your PR on a workout. Typically, the wider the trainer’s base, the more stable it will be. Many have a leveling feature for uneven surfaces.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8869. What Is a Timeshare? Why Financial Experts Say Avoid Them

A timeshare is a shared ownership or usage right in a vacation property. You pay an upfront purchase price — typically $20,000 to $40,000 — plus annual maintenance fees that currently average $1,120 per year and increase 3-5% annually. In exchange, you get the right to use a resort unit for a specific period each year, usually one week.

The timeshare industry generates over $10 billion in annual sales, and roughly 9.9 million U.S. households own at least one timeshare. But ownership satisfaction varies dramatically, and the financial reality rarely matches the sales presentation delivered during high-pressure resort tours.

Deeded (Fixed Week): You own a fractional interest in a specific unit during a specific week each year. This is actual real property — you receive a deed, it's recorded with the county, and you can theoretically sell, rent, or bequeath it. The problem: the secondary market for these deeds values most of them at near zero.

Right-to-Use (Leased): You purchase the right to use a property for a set number of years (typically 20-40 years) but don't own real estate. At the end of the term, your usage right expires with nothing to show for it. This is common with newer resort brands.

Points-Based Systems: Instead of a fixed week at a fixed resort, you purchase an annual allotment of points that can be redeemed at various properties within a resort network. Flexibility is the selling point, but availability at popular destinations during peak seasons is often limited — and points can inflate over time, requiring more points for the same week.

Timeshare companies spend an average of $4,000 in marketing costs per sale — and much of that goes toward the high-pressure sales presentations that are a signature of the industry. These presentations use urgency tactics ("this price is only available today"), comparison anchoring (showing the cost per vacation day), and emotional triggers ("don't you want the best for your family?"). The FI community's rule: never make a five-figure financial decision on the same day you learn about it. Walk away, run the numbers at home, and compare alternatives. The offer will still be available tomorrow — despite what the salesperson claims.

Timeshare sales presentations focus on the purchase price and the "cost per vacation night." What they don't emphasize is the total lifetime cost, which includes mandatory annual fees that increase every year, special assessments for major repairs, exchange fees if you want to trade your week, and the opportunity cost of that capital.

Let's run the real numbers on a typical timeshare over 20 years:

At $4,204 per week over 20 years — without accounting for the opportunity cost of the capital — you can book luxury vacation rentals in most destinations for less money with zero long-term commitment.

This is the most important financial fact about timeshares: they have almost no resale value. The American Resort Development Association (ARDA) — the timeshare industry's own trade group — acknowledges that resale prices are a fraction of the original purchase price. In practice, most timeshares on the secondary market are listed for $1 or even offered for free, because the buyer inherits the mandatory annual maintenance fees.

Websites like RedWeek, TUG (Timeshare Users Group), and eBay are filled with timeshare listings at $0-$1. Owners often can't give them away because the ongoing fee obligation makes them a liability, not an asset. This is the fundamental difference between a timeshare and a real investment: real investments appreciate or generate income. Timeshares depreciate to zero and generate mandatory ongoing costs.

If you already own a timeshare and want out, here are your realistic options:

Rescission Period: Most states give you 3-15 days after purchase to cancel without penalty. This is your best exit — if you're within this window, cancel immediately in writing via certified mail.

Sell on the Resale Market: List on TUG (Timeshare Users Group), RedWeek, or eBay. Set your expectations: you'll likely sell for $0-$1, and the "sale" is really about transferring the maintenance fee obligation to a willing buyer.

Contact the Resort's Deed-Back Program: Some major resort chains (Wyndham, Marriott, Hilton) offer deed-back or surrender programs where you can return the timeshare to the resort. Eligibility varies and there may be fees, but this is a legitimate exit path.

Timeshare Exit Companies: Proceed with Extreme Caution. The timeshare exit industry is plagued with scams. Legitimate exit attorneys exist, but many "exit companies" charge $3,000-$10,000 upfront and deliver nothing. The FTC and state attorneys general have pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Before hiring anyone, check their BBB rating, look for complaints with your state attorney general, and never pay the full fee upfront.

The FI community has consistently found that travel rewards credit cards, vacation rental platforms, and strategic booking provide better vacation value than timeshare ownership:

Here's the number that should end the timeshare debate for any FI-focused person: the average timeshare's annual maintenance fee ($1,120) invested in index funds at a 10% average return grows to $72,000+ in 20 years and $203,000+ in 30 years. Add the opportunity cost of the $24,140 purchase price invested instead, and the 30-year FI impact exceeds $440,000. That's nearly half a million dollars diverted from your FI number for one week of vacation per year at a resort you didn't choose.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Travel well, spend less, keep your FI timeline intact.

Choose a card that matches your spending patterns and offers flexible points or transferable miles. Sign-up bonuses alone often cover 1-2 free flights or hotel stays in the first year.

Pro tip: Pay the balance in full every month. Travel rewards only work financially if you never carry a balance and pay interest.

Instead of paying $1,120/year in mandatory timeshare fees, deposit that same amount monthly ($93/month) into a high-yield savings account earmarked for travel. You'll have $1,120+ per year to spend on any vacation, anywhere.

Research destinations on Airbnb, VRBO, and Booking.com. Booking 3-6 months ahead gets the best selection. Compare total costs including cleaning fees and service charges to timeshare equivalent costs.

Shifting your vacation by 2-4 weeks outside peak season saves 30-50% on flights and accommodation. Shoulder season often has better weather than peak season with fewer crowds.

If you were considering a $24,000 timeshare purchase, invest that money instead. At 10% average returns, $24,000 grows to $62,000 in 10 years and $161,000 in 20 years — all while you vacation on your own terms.

Pro tip: Set up automatic monthly investments for the amount you would have spent on timeshare financing payments.

A timeshare's purchase price ($24,140) plus 30 years of maintenance fees ($1,120/year growing at 3.5%) totals over $83,000 in direct costs. Invested in index funds at 10% average returns instead, that same money grows to over $440,000. That's the true cost of a timeshare — not the sticker price, but nearly half a million dollars of lost wealth-building potential over a career.

No. A timeshare is a prepaid vacation plan, not an investment. Timeshares depreciate to near-zero resale value, generate mandatory ongoing costs that increase annually, and cannot produce income for the owner in most cases. The timeshare industry itself has moved away from calling them investments because of regulatory scrutiny.

The average annual maintenance fee is $1,120, according to ARDA (the industry trade group). Fees increase an average of 3-5% per year and are mandatory — you must pay them whether or not you use your timeshare. Some resort areas (Hawaii, ski towns) charge $1,500-$2,500+ per year. Special assessments for major repairs can add $1,000-$5,000 in any given year.

Technically yes, but practically it's very difficult. The secondary market is flooded with inventory at $0-$1 prices because most owners are trying to escape their maintenance fee obligations. Resale companies that promise to sell your timeshare for thousands of dollars are almost always scams. The most realistic options are deed-back to the resort, transfer to a willing buyer at $0-$1, or working with a licensed timeshare exit attorney.

The resort will send your account to collections, report the delinquency to credit bureaus (damaging your credit score), and potentially pursue legal action. For deeded timeshares, the resort can foreclose on the property. Maintenance fee obligations are contractual and legally enforceable — you cannot simply walk away without consequences.

Some are, many are not. The FTC has pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Red flags include: demanding full payment ($3,000-$10,000) upfront, guaranteeing results, using high-pressure sales tactics similar to timeshare presentations, and lack of BBB accreditation. If you need exit help, consult a licensed real estate attorney in the state where the timeshare is located.

In very narrow circumstances: if you genuinely vacation at the same resort every year, the annual cost (maintenance fees amortized with purchase price) is lower than booking that same unit independently, and you purchased on the resale market for $0-$1 (avoiding the $24,000+ retail markup). Even then, you're locked into one destination with escalating fees. For most people, the flexibility and cost advantage of alternatives makes timeshares a poor choice.

A timeshare is a prepaid vacation plan with a near-zero resale value, mandatory escalating fees, and an extremely difficult exit process. The average timeshare costs over $84,000 across 20 years of ownership — and that money invested instead could grow to over $440,000 in 30 years. Modern alternatives like travel rewards cards, vacation rentals, and strategic off-peak booking deliver comparable or better vacation experiences with zero long-term commitment. If you're building toward financial independence, a timeshare is one of the most damaging financial products you can buy. #8868. Less Cars, More Money: My Visit to the City of the Future

In my role as Mr. Money Mustache, I do my best to be your one-stop-shop for Lifestyle Guru ideas. So over the years we’ve covered not just the Money side of life, but also the even more important stuff like health and fitness and the psychology of better, happier living.

But there’s one single area of life where all of these factors come together with an almost Nuclear Fusion level of synergy and effectiveness. And because of that, if I could have one single wish in the world, this is what I would wish for. It’s a change so massive that it would make every person on the planet better off and fix most of our problems in one grand sweep. And it’s probably not what you’d expect:

That we immediately switch to building our cities and countries around people, instead of cars.

(and then fix all of our existing ones too, so that our entire world is built around person-friendly living.)

The benefits of this are way bigger than almost anyone can imagine. We’re not just talking about eliminating a bit of pollution or a few traffic jams or car crashes. No. This is about far richer, healthier, and most importantly more fun living for everyone.

To put even conservative numbers to this, we’re talking about a life boost of over $20,000 per person per year, which compounds into well over two million dollars per adult lifetime.

On a nationwide scale, this would boost the wealth of the United States by about seven trillion dollars per year, which would compound into about 770 trillion over the next five decades.

Which happens to be more than the current total amount of human wealth on the entire planet.

You will have a house that is both cheaper and more beautiful and spacious. Your body and brain will be healthier and stronger and sexier and cost a lot less time and healthcare dollars to maintain.

And all of our wallets and investment accounts, both public and private will be absolutely overflowing with surplus income, reduced expenses, and fuel an investment and prosperity boom like the world has never seen.

“Isn’t city planning just a stuffy thing that your city council does in the background while we’re all off living our lives?”

Well, yes it is right now. And that’s the whole problem: cities are built by people whose primary job is to maintain the status quo and prevent disruptions. And those committes are elected and encouraged by crusty old companies and organizations, and plain old grumpy neighbors who just don’t have the vision to see what they are missing.

I’m convinced that if everyone could see through the smoggy haze of the status quo, we would all agree that this idea of a radical change is not only the best idea, but the only reasonable idea to even consider.

So our job is to learn and explain just how big and how easy this is. And what it boils down to is pretty damned simple.

So for the same amount of space you can have an entire pretty nice two bedroom apartment, or you can have just enough space for two (small) cars to park and pull out. But it gets even crazier than this. Check out this random intersection here in my own city:

WHAT?! So every time you have two big car roads intersect, which happens hundreds of times in every big city, you are wasting enough space to build a luxurious, resort-like living area with about one hundred two-bedroom apartments and still have room for a pool, a dog park, a grocery store, a couple of restaurants, and so on.

This is just the beginning of the insanity, because I have only shown you two parking spaces and one intersection. The reality is that our entire cities are made almost entirely of stupid, expensive wasted space like this.

And the problem is so extreme that the only reason we think we need cars to get around, is because we have wasted most of our space on accommodating cars, which spread everything out so far (and made everything so loud and dangerous) that nobody feels like walking or biking!

Whenever you propose any great new idea, you’ll always get a bunch of smartasses who like to complain and resist change, without even bothering to think it through.

“But how are we going to keep driving our cars just as much as we do now?”

Which is ridiculous – because the whole point is that as soon as you cut out all the huge wasted spaces we create to accommodate cars, you are suddenly FREE from needing cars so much!

Instead, you can just weave a brand new city, with a bunch of variations of this beautiful resort which also include offices, grocery stores, climbing gyms and every other amenity.

And yes, you’d still have some roads between them, but they would be mostly for deliveries, emergency vehicles and people who need mobility assistance.

I hope you’re not going to make me ride the bus?

I am all for public transit in theory, but to be honest I don’t usually have the patience for it. I don’t do lineups, and I don’t like to stand around waiting passively for my transportation to arrive – when it’s time to go somewhere, I just want to go, and go now, and get there fast. So my own personal choice is to take a bike for short distances (under 2 miles) or an e-bike for larger ones (up to about 15 miles).

Although this is often news to car drivers, bikes are much faster than cars for urban transport, plus they give me exercise and thrill, which is way better than being stuck at the red light with the cars.

If you take this already-superior method of urban transport and cut out the 90% of the land that we waste on accommodating the inferior cars, then you end up with a revolution: everybody gets where they are going ten times faster, at much lower cost, and has much more fun doing it.

And sure, there will also be light rail and faster buses. And sure, you can still hop in an Uber or even bring your own car into a city like this.But the point is that it will just happen much much less often.

Okay I’m convinced, but how can we actually accomplish this?

Mr. Money Mustache can talk a big game with all these fancy words and pictures, but the truth is that I’m way too impatient to put up with all the bureaucracy and complaints that arise when you try to actually change a city. I’ve been doing my best here in Longmont, and I have gotten just about nowhere. We’re still just stacking on more and more layers of ridiculous car shit where I live.

Thankfully, other people are much more patient and effective than I am at affecting change, and one group has made such incredible progress that you can now go LIVE in their first creation: a 1000-person car-free neighborhood called Culdesac Tempe. And as I write this, I am staying in a hotel right nearby, having spent the past two days touring and visiting and interviewing the founders*.

While we were at it, my Phoenix-area-house-fixing friend Tracy Royce and I also hosted a meetup for an enthusiastic group of our readers/viewers right there in Culdesac’s emerging central plaza.

Culdesac is Awesome and Could Change Everything

If you only look at the financial spreadsheet, you would think this first Culdesac project is just going to be a highly profitable 1000-person cluster of apartment buildings, spread out across 17 acres of land. And while financial sustainability is indeed a key reason why this model will succeed, the money is the least exciting part.

When you look at these pictures compared to a normal housing complex, the main thing you will notice is that all the space that would normally be wasted on parking lots, is instead used for beautiful walking and gathering areas.

The next big upgrade is that they mixed in the amenities for daily life right into the neighborhood, rather than forcing all the future residents to get into their cars to drive out to find them:

I was also impressed with just the feel of walking the Mediterranean-vibed spaces between the buildings, even at this early stage when everything is still under construction.

Due to the hot desert climate of the region, everything is built around providing shade, breeze, and reflecting heat during the summer, while also maximizing the joyful fact that there is no winter there (the coldest month of the year still has an average daily high of 65F/18C, which means palm trees, leafy gardens and fruits and flowers forever.)

With a setup like this, and 999 new neighbors to meet, I would rarely feel the need to leave the place. Which really cuts down on my desire to use a car. But on top of that, Culdesac has strategically placed itself in Tempe, a city right in the center of the Phoenix metro area, within walking distance of the main university and right on a light rail stop which allows you to reach almost everything (including the airport) for FREE, since an annual pass to the transit system is included with your rent.

But of course, you can also get around on foot, bike, e-bike, scooter, or hop into one of Culdesac’s fleet of rideshare electric cars for a trip to the mountains or whatever else you might want to do that’s outside of bike and transit range.

It’s insane. In fact it’s so good that I am going to attempt to move there myself at the end of 2023, enjoying my first escape from Colorado winter and celebrating the fact that my boy will be a legal adult at that time.

But even this is just a pilot project because Culdesac has much bigger plans.

From my conversations with the founders, I think they want to do this:

So How Can We Benefit From This, and Support it?

This whole change is exciting, and it is immense.

Understanding these ideas around city planning is the economic and social equivalent to being a doctor, and finding a 35-year-old patient in a hospital who is suffering from every chronic disease, but then discovering that they have been following a diet of Coke and Donuts for their whole lives and never been out on a walk, once.

In other words, the changes are so obvious, and the amount of win/win synergy so great, that every step we take towards making our cities better, and every car trip we eliminate, will absolutely explode our personal and national wealth upwards for generations to come.

Another collaborator in the overall effort for car free cities is a bank-founding multi entrepreneur local friend named Kevin Dahlstrom. His recent Twitter rant on building car-free cities from the scratch gathered a shocking amount of very positive feedback and interesting comments.

* Despite my positive raving about this neighborhood, I have no financial or business connection with the project or any of the team members. I am just really excited about their work and want them to succeed!

Mr. Money Mustache April 7, 2023, 4:27 pm

Good point Stephanie – I believe that part is coming soon, as the first batch of apartments open up and are ready for rent (right now you are only signing up for the waiting list rather than an actual apartment).

Since I was there and asked the same question in person, the answer is basically “market rate” – in other words, when a new apartment goes up for rent, the builders typically conduct a price survey of what would be a competitive price at that moment, and then they start advertising at that price.

Just like any other supply and demand sensitive thing, these prices will then fluctuate based on the demand level until you lock it in with a lease. During my tour, it was a hot time for rentals in prosperous Tempe so the rent was around $2.50 per square foot per month, or a little under $2k for a large 1-bedroom apartment.

Note that at Culdesac you get a few extra perks included in that rent: internet access that works across the whole 17 acre campus, gym, pool, and unlimited transit pass along with credits for bike and carshare as well.

Believe it or not, this is not a big problem in Phoenix and most other big desert cities. They have plenty of water for domestic use. It’s agriculture that uses the lion’s share of fresh water – about 80% of it in the Western US. Then our other industrial uses, then our houses are down near the bottom.

One major improvement in places like Phoenix and Las Vegas versus the rest of the country is that they have managed to mostly eliminate suburban lawns. A single patch of lawn watered in the desert will use more than an entire household, so as soon as you remove that you have made the whole city more sustainable.

Alas, here in the Denver area the lawn with the big sprinkler system still seems to be in style, despite the fact that our summer climate very closely resembles a real desert. The grass will die within a week or two if you leave it unwatered, which I think would be a great idea in most cases. There’s lots of cool stuff you can do with river rocks and native flowers and Yucca plants that takes almost no water to sustain!

#8867. Inside Sullivan Middaugh’s Balancing Act Between Off-Road Dominance and LA 2028

There are few races Sullivan Middaugh would like to target more than next year’s XTERRA World Championship in New Mexico. However, if everything goes to plan, there’s only a slim chance he’ll be on the start line to defend his title.

That’s because Middaugh is part of an exciting crop of American men trying to help the Project Podium program live up to its name at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. And with an increasingly crowded triathlon calendar, the timing doesn’t quite work.

The challenge is that the 2027 XTERRA World Championship weekend in Ruidoso falls between the World Triathlon Championship Finals in Hamburg, Germany, and another top-level race in Weihai, China. Both are part of the rebranded T50 Championship series.

Not only could these events prove critical in helping the U.S. secure three men’s spots for Los Angeles – the host nation is already guaranteed two – but Hamburg could also present an opportunity for Middaugh to stake his claim to one of those places.

He can’t afford to let up. It’s still early in the Olympic qualification cycle, but the U.S. currently has eight men in the top 50 of the Olympic rankings, more than any other nation, with Middaugh the fourth-ranked American at 31st overall.

But while the focus will understandably shift toward the work of coach Parker Spencer’s Project Podium squad, which splits its time between Tempe, Arizona, in the winter and Park City, Utah, in the summer, XTERRA will never be entirely out of mind.

After all, it’s the discipline that put the Middaugh family on the triathlon map, and never more so than earlier this month, when Sullivan claimed his first full-distance XTERRA world title, younger brother Porter finished seventh, and father Josiah, at 48 years young, placed sixth.

Three members of the same family, spanning two generations, finishing in the top seven of a World Championship race is a remarkable feat, with few obvious parallels across elite sport.

The achievement was even more special because it had been 11 years since an American man last won the event. That was Josiah, in 2015. Before him, you have to go back another 15 years to Michael Tobin’s victory in 2000.

“No, I haven’t heard anything quite like that,” Sullivan confirms. “And especially having my dad in the race is pretty incredible!”

More than the result itself, it’s the opportunity to continue racing alongside his father that Sullivan appreciates.

“Following in his footsteps is pretty awesome,” he continues. “Every year he says he’s gonna retire, but I don’t know. It’s been pretty awesome to be able to continue to train and race with him. I grew up just following him on the XTERRA circuit and going to races and watching him. I never really thought we’d be racing together.”

Sullivan’s success also made up for his defeat by Reed Legg at the North American Championship earlier this year. Legg’s victory interrupted a Middaugh dynasty that has seen Josiah win 15 U.S. elite national titles and Sullivan dominate the more recent championship era.

And it was made all the sweeter by the XTERRA World Championship’s return to the U.S. after four years in Italy.

“I put it on my calendar and kept it in mind all year,” Sullivan says. “It was a race at altitude, which I grew up at, and so I felt like it was a good opportunity. Grindstone Lake, where we swam, is at 7,000 feet and the course got up to maybe a little bit over 8,000 feet. But at home in Colorado, my house is at like 7,500 feet, and you can only really go up from there. So, the six or seven weeks leading in, I went home and trained with dad because I knew it would be a big advantage if I could be fully acclimatized.”

While Porter, who also trains with Project Podium, finished seventh, Sullivan believes his younger brother might have mounted a stronger challenge had he not been racing at the Under-23 World Championship in Spain.

Sullivan skipped that race to sharpen his mountain biking skills, although it didn’t prevent an early spill on the bike.

“Yeah, I overcooked the corners a little bit on the first couple of turns in the single track section,” he explains. “It wasn’t a bad spill out, but I kinda had to slam on the brake, go off the trail, tip over and get up quick. My bike computer fell off, which wasn’t a big deal, and maybe a blessing in disguise to not worry about power and just focus on effort.”

Sullivan had an almost four-minute lead heading onto the run and extended his advantage with the day’s fastest 10K split, but at no point did he feel comfortable.

“I didn’t really get any splits and thought that no lead was safe on the run. I just tried to give it full gas, focusing on pushing the climbs and rolling the downhills because I knew they’d be coming.”

Among the athletes trying to hunt him down were two very familiar faces – Porter and Josiah – and there was a brief moment of family camaraderie as their paths crossed on the course.

“I just focus on myself for the most part, but it reminds you that they’re also out there battling. I saw them running together, so that was pretty cool because I knew they’d be pushing each other. We were all pumped, gave each other a high five, and that was pretty much it.”

There were plenty more high fives and hugs at the finish, where Sullivan’s mom, sister, and grandparents were also in attendance.

While this was Sullivan’s first full-distance XTERRA world title, he had previously won the Short Track World Championship in Molveno, Italy, in 2024.

In recent years, short-track racing has typically taken place a couple of days before or the day after the main event, although it wasn’t on the schedule in Ruidoso.

“It’s like a three or four-minute swim, maybe a 15-minute bike and a seven-minute run,” Sullivan says, with distances depending on the course layout. “It’s all under 30 minutes for the most part, so more intense and a little bit different, and you can’t make as many mistakes. I think it suits me because I’ve spent a lot of time training for sprint distance draft-legal triathlons. I really enjoy it.”

While XTERRA might be seen as a distraction from road triathlon, Sullivan believes it complements his efforts elsewhere.

“It helps me with my skills for the draft-legal stuff as well. I look to people like Flora Duffy and Hayden Wilde who were able to do well at both, and think they’re an example for me.”

For the next 18 months, the priority will be collecting Olympic qualification points, with the window having opened in May.

Sullivan has already recorded top-10 finishes at World Triathlon Cups in Huatulco, Mexico; Edmonton, Canada; Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; and Asunción, Paraguay. He also competed at the Americas Triathlon Championships in Antofagasta, Chile, finishing 11th. He now heads to Chile for two more World Cup races, in San Pedro de la Paz and Iquique.

While USA Triathlon hasn’t officially released its selection policy for Los Angeles, Sullivan expects the Olympic test event in July 2027 and the World Championship Finals in Hamburg to be key races. He anticipates that a top-eight finish, combined with being the leading American, could be enough to meet the automatic selection criteria.

But first, he needs to secure starts at the biggest races. “Spots keep flipping, so it’s gonna be pretty tough,” he adds. “I’ve been mostly focusing on the World Cup level, which is the step below the World Championship Series, but as my swim develops, I’ll try and focus more on the World Championship Series because that’s the level you need to be at in the Olympics.”

The higher the level, the more critical the swim becomes. “If you’re the best swimmer, you can be in the race up until the run, but if you don’t have a good swim, you may never even be in the race,” he explains. “The swim sets you up for a good day to get in the right bike group, but you also need to be able to run well off a hard bike. That’s something XTERRA helps me with.”

Sullivan admits that bridging the gap in the swim is his biggest immediate challenge, but he also knows he’ll need a blistering run to compete at the very top.

“Especially with Alex Yee and Hayden Wilde, it is just getting faster and faster,” he says. “You need to be an elite runner if you want to be on the podium, and that means hitting sub-14 minutes sometimes in the 5K and sub-29 minutes occasionally on the 10K. Right now, I’m in the low 14s and around 30, maybe a little under depending on the course.”

If he can get there, it will be with the help of Project Podium. Established in 2018, Project Podium is funded by USA Triathlon, corporate sponsors, and private donors, including longtime benefactors Dr. Bill Warren and his wife Lynne. Based at Arizona State University, the program provides promising American male triathletes with coaching, scholarships, and financial support as they pursue Olympic ambitions.

Sullivan, who graduated with a degree in biomedical sciences in August, has enormous respect for coach Spencer, who he says also understands his passion for the trails and why XTERRA should remain part of his program.

“I love mountain biking, and so it’s good for me to be able to kinda go in and out, but I think that as the Olympics get closer I’ll have to take a slight step away from XTERRA, but we’ll see.”

Finally, if Sullivan’s Olympic dream does come to fruition, could there be more than one Middaugh on the U.S. team?

“That’s definitely a big ask, but would be amazing. I don’t know if it’s on the cards for ’28, but maybe for ’32 it could be more plausible. I think we both have the ability to get to that level if we stick with it, and when I see Porter in the race, we don’t really need to say anything. We just understand what we need to do.”

#8866. The 10 Best Running Shoes for Wide Feet and Big Toes

Don’t subject yourself to cramped feet—these running shoes are the comfiest and roomiest.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

I’m four miles out on my run when I feel angry blisters forming between my toes because they’re overcrowded in my shoe’s toebox. Add that to a long list of annoying things going on with my feet: mild plantar fasciitis, black toenails, gnarly calluses that make me ashamed to wear sandals. I am a card-carrying member of the wide-foot club, yet I’ve resisted wide-width running shoes for years. Mostly because around the time I found I had wide feet (over 15 years ago), the only colors available in wide-widths were black, white, or gray.

Today, running shoes for wide feet have become more accessible, more visible, and less boring. Perhaps with the dawn of foot scans at specialty running shops, store owners and brands are finally realizing just how common wide-footed runners are—and why it’s so important runners stop squishing their feet in standard-sized shoes.

I’ve run 28 marathons and vet all kinds of gear, from sports bras to smartwatches, as RW running reviews editor. For research, I visited Aardvark Sports Shop, a local run store in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, to get the lowdown on running shoes for wide-foot runners from Aardvark Footwear Lead Trainer Kate Egging. Egging, a former RW wear-tester, has worked at Aardvark for four years and is a lifelong wide-foot runner, like myself. I also spoke with A. Stacie Page, PT, DPT, of Johns Hopkins Running Program at Johns Hopkins Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, who discussed the risks of wearing too-narrow shoes and how this can affect running performance.

Besides gear expertise provided by our staff, we also have a team of 300-plus local shoe testers who log at least 100 miles per pair of running shoes. They provide valuable feedback on fit, feel, and ride to help us determine the best trainers, ensuring our selections are all-inclusive. We also enlisted the help of Egging, because she gets to try on shoes at Aardvark and help runners make footwear decisions.

Compared to the Brooks Ghost, the Brooks Glycerin is broader in the midfoot area, resulting in a more accommodating fit for wider foot shapes. The new triple jacquard knit also provides a stretchier upper that houses wide feet.

The midsole foam provides a supportive, high-energy-return ride stacked at 38 mm in the heel. Brooks added 2 mm of DNA Tuned in the forefoot. What you get is more balanced cushioning throughout the shoe and a lower heel-toe drop.

I’ve worn the Glycerin 23 for base miles and long runs. My feet fit securely in the shoe thanks to the padded border on the interior of the heel collar. The softness underfoot and overall cozy fit make the Glycerin 23 a preferred everyday shoe in my testing pile and one I can depend on when I’m scheduled for hours on the road, according to my training plan.

Shop Men’s at brooksrunning.com | Shop Women’s at brooksrunning.com

It was a tough choice for Senior Editor Pavlína Černá, when she had to choose a shoe to wear for a 75K march south of Prague in the Czech Republic. Her decision: the On Cloudmonster 3.

“The signature CloudTec sole absorbs the impact of my steps like it’s a tiny trampoline that pushes me off right away and rocks me forward, doing half the work of running (or walking) for me,” she said in her shoe review (link below). “The toebox is wide and slightly stretchy, accommodating my foot as it swells over time.”

At Aardvark, Egging noted how On’s shoes have a surprisingly wide but secure fit. Several of our testers also praised the shoe for its roomy toebox.

The shoe has a Speedboard to promote propulsion. The source of its high rebound comes from its Helion foam and CloudTec system. We liked the overall comfort of the shoe on walks, long hikes, and daily runs.

“[The shoe] is super comfortable, excellent cushioning, nothing pinched rubbed or anything,” said tester Dave Brattley. “Definitely, the best pair of shoes that I have had the chance to run in.”

One thing to note: The shoe is only available in standard size. But we found the broad platform and lacing system make the Cloudmonster 3 accessible for both wide- and narrow-foot runners.

Shop Men’s at on.com | Shop Women’s at on.com

What? A Nike shoe on our Best Running Shoes for Wide Feet list? Expecting the brand’s usual narrow fit when I got my pair of Vomero 18s to test I was shocked how accommodating the fit felt wrapped around my wide feet.

Nike updated the lasts of its popular franchises—the Vomero, Structure, and Alphafly—basing the wider foot shape on women’s feedback. Turns out both women and men liked the end result.

The shoe is mega plush with 46 mm of ZoomX and ReactX foams, making it an ideal pick for long runs. The ride is soft and responsive, like a Brooks Glycerin or Saucony Triumph—but with PEBA.

“I really enjoyed how incredibly comfortable the Vomero 18 was,” said Editorial Assistant Michael McDonough. “Once the shoes were broken in, the sheer volume of cushion made longer runs much more enjoyable and pain-free. They helped me increase my mileage without hurting my feet, which has been an issue for me in the past.”

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com

The Gel-Kayano 33 introduces a new stability system: FluidSupport. Replacing the 4-D Guidance system, FluidSupport involves the dual-foam midsole—FF Blast Max and FF Blast Plus—working in tandem with the shoe’s geometry to help guide your form when you need it. The shoe is more flexible with FluidSupport, despite the 40 mm of beefy cushioning.

The shoe only comes in standard size, but it offers plenty of space for runners with high insteps, along with a snug fit in the midfoot area. I found the shoe to have ample toe room. My wide feet didn’t feel squeezed nor did my instep feel any pressure on my runs. Running in the Gel-Kayano 33, you won’t have to stop to loosen the laces.

Our wide-foot testers shared similar feedback. “I like the upper; the collar has lots of cushion that didn’t irritate my ankle bone,” said Lorenzo Molina. “The lacing system was smooth and the overall fit is great because my foot fits better in a wider shoe.”

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com

Just about everything about the Guide 19 is accommodating. It preserves the same soft, cushioned feel as its predecessor with the same unobtrusive stability tech for, yes, guiding erratic running form.

CenterPath tech lends stability with higher sidewalls and a broader base. The Pwrrun midsole provides max-cushioning, making the Guide 19 a terrific long-run and recovery shoe of choice.

One tester gave the trainer his highest rating because of “its strong comfort, support, and cushioning, and the fact that it had no major weaknesses.”

“I was lucky enough to test this shoe’s predecessor, the Saucony Guide 18, and I enjoyed that shoe immensely for the same reasons,” said our tester, Dave Block. “But I think this model has even more cushioning and softness.”

Shop Men’s at saucony.com | Shop Women’s at saucony.com

The Torin 9 showcases several updates that make the daily trainer an even more welcoming intro to zero-drop shoes. The 28 mm stack height houses the brand’s P35X foam, with a dense core and soft carrier that softens landings without masking ground feel.

“I generally prefer cushioning that provides protection without disconnecting me from the running experience, and the Torin strikes that balance exceptionally well,” said tester Don Kuntzman. “The cushioning felt evenly distributed from heel to forefoot, creating a smooth, balanced ride that never felt overly soft, mushy, or unstable.”

The outsole has Vibram rubber, making the shoe’s ride tackier and more versatile. Our testers weren’t afraid to traverse onto the trail after hitting pace on the road.

The non-gusseted tongue provides more room for high insteps. Altra’s signature wide toebox is a bunion-prone, wide-foot runner’s dream. No need to worry about rubbing or hot spots.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

Last year, Egging said the Clifton 10 was a pleasant surprise in terms of fit for wide feet. Unlike the Bondi 9, which has a narrower fit than past iterations, she found the Clifton 10’s sidewalls non-intrusive and the midfoot non-constrictive. The same goes for the Clifton 11. Hoka didn’t narrow the shoe’s fit, and it feels just as comfy and accommodating as its predecessor.

The shoe has Hoka’s Active Foot Frame to cradle your foot and help with stability. This means you can run and walk in the Clifton 11 confidently without rolling your ankles or feeling confined and stiff with extra stability features.

The compression-molded EVA foam isn’t as responsive as other supercritical foams you see in running shoes, but the Clifton 11 still has a high energy return ride that boosts everyday runs, long runs, and run/walks.

Shop Men’s at hoka.com | Shop Women’s at hoka.com

Egging wants everyone to know the Echelon 10 is not like the old Echelons Saucony was known for. Formerly a clunky run/walker for runners who need orthotics, the tenth iteration is lighter and more nimble, yet still orthotic-friendly. The shoe has the brand’s highly responsive Pwrrun midsole, which is the same foam in the Guide 18.

According to Egging, the Echelon 10 is an excellent choice for underpronators, or supinators (when your foot rolls inward less than 15 percent while running), because of its broad base and comfy cushioning.

“The Echelon gets a little bit overlooked because it falls into such a ‘comfort customer’ category,” Egging says. “But if you’ve got that new runner that has a high volume foot, maybe that 4E runner who needs the extra wide, who supinates and they need a broader base, this shoe is very runnable.”

If you are having issues with other trainers or are a new runner with specific needs, don’t discredit the Echelon 10. It could be your ticket to a great ride

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com

Brands tend to make super shoes more tapered in the midfoot, like the spiked shoes on a track. But the Rocket X 3 has an accommodating, broad platform that you could slide an orthotic into.

The shoe has dual-density PEBA foam and a winged carbon plate to promote propulsion. The upper is single-layer engineered mesh, which allows for breathability over the course of a sweaty, foot-swelling marathon. It was tester Shane Houghton’s favorite feature.

“The mesh upper is a great part about Rocket X 2,” he said. “When you tighten the shoe it stays securely in place and wraps around your foot perfectly. And it’s so airy and breathable because the holes in the netting are so big. There is no chance of your feet getting hot in these shoes no matter how tight you’re wearing them. I appreciated the padding around the heel. It was nice to have that there when a lot of racers don’t.”

The Lone Peak 9+ offers both a comfy fit with a roomy toebox, providing ample room for toe splaying. “Fit and comfort is something that the Lone Peak 9+ has dialed in,” says Rip Cantelmi, who previously tested the Lone Peak 7 and Brooks Divide 5. “Laced up, the foot feels relaxed, strong, and sensitive. I have observed that the shoe is wide enough to accommodate toe spacers if you use them. The padding around the collar remains optimized for comfort and flexibility. Heat management remains positive.”

The Altra Lone Peak 9+ has an Altra Ego midsole, which provides just enough supportive cushioning as well as some ground feel, which testers like Cantelmi appreciated.

“Ground feel is something that many trail shoes ignore for the pursuit of comfort in the form of high-stacked foam, but the Lone Peak 9+ finds the perfect balance of cushion, protection, and feel,” says Cantelmi, who describes the shoe’s cushioning as neither minimalist nor marshmallowy.

Shop Men’s at altra.com | Shop Women’s at altra.com

Misconceptions About Wide-Foot Runners and Shoes

“I’ve had my feet measured before; I don’t need to do it again”

Getting your foot measured is not a once-and-done kind of deal. Your foot size changes throughout your life, due to aging, work, and having children. “Sometimes when people get pregnant their feet sizes change dramatically,” says Page. “An injury could also cause an arch to drop if you don’t have that same muscle activation.”

She references a study on incorrectly fitted footwear published in 2018, which found a large proportion of the population was wearing the incorrect size shoe and how this can be associated with foot pain and foot disorders. Her recommendation is simple: get a comfortable shoe that fits properly.

Another reason to have your foot scanned: Some runners may think they have a wide foot when in actuality they have a high arch or instep. “That’s when they need a shoe measuring that high profile,” says Egging.

“I’ve worn this shoe forever; the newest version will fit the same”

“I think it might be even more important for a wide-footed runner to revisit a run specialty store for a fit because the models as they update, don’t always fit the same,” says Egging.

The Hoka Bondi 9, for example, fits narrower than the previous iteration. This is because of Hoka’s sidewalls which are built up to hug your foot, which can result in a tighter fit for wide-foot Bondi lovers.

Altra also requires some probing. Even though the brand is known for its accommodating footshapes and roomy toeboxes, some Altra shoes can fit narrower in the midfoot due to updates. Upper “upgrades” to look out for in any kind of shoe when you’re a wide-foot shopper are gusseted tongues, which can make the fit tighter due to more material on the instep, and overlays.

“Getting black toenails is a rite of passage”

Black toenails are not a badge of honor. Egging is an ultrarunner and she’s never lost one toenail because she received a proper shoe fitting early in her run career. Other signs of needing to get refitted and change your shoe size: numbness, tingling, Achilles tendonitis, and plantar fasciitis.

“Movement is good!” Egging says, when runners are concerned about a little looseness in a road shoe. “A lot of plantar fasciitis in wide-foot runners is coming from that arch being crunched by tight-fitting shoes.” (Trail shoes are a different story; you’ll want a more secure hold around your foot.) Tightness and constriction can also negatively affect your performance. That kind of discomfort, Page warns, can change your running pattern and lead to pain or injury.

When it comes to choosing running shoes, you want some wiggle room. If you see bruising, blood blisters on the tops of your toes, or experience toe curling, you probably need a wider toebox—this also includes runners with hammertoes, bunions, bunionettes, and Morton’s neuroma.

With your bare foot, step on a blank piece of paper. Outline your foot with a pen or pencil. Use a ruler to measure the widest part in inches of your stencil horizontally (across the ball of your foot); be aware you’ll need a wider toebox if you have bunions or bunionettes. Write this number down and refer to the men’s or women’s chart to find your width

Related: How to measure your feet: A guide for runners

What can I do when the shoe I want to buy isn’t available in wide?

If you’re a bra wearer, you may have heard the term “sister sizes.” Shoes also have sister sizes. For example, I wear women’s 5.5 in street shoes, but most of my running shoes are 6.5 because they’re the standard width (B). I size up for foot swelling (it’s recommended to size up your running shoes) and size up again for width. I’m actually a size 6, C width in women’s running shoes.

It’ll take several try-ons to get the right feel and the right shoe, but it can be possible to find a women’s B or men’s D size shoe if there are no wides available, or wide if your foot is extra wide. Women can also pivot to a men’s size, but be forewarned: men’s shoes tend to run longer and have more space in the heel area.

“Socks are super, super important,” says Egging. “I think people neglect that. The price point is frightening at first. You’re like, $18 for one pair of socks? That’s insane! But eight years later when you still have that same sock and that six-pack you got at T.J. Maxx has come and gone in the meantime.” She recommends Injinji, Blister Resist, and Balega.

At RW HQ, we’ve been testing Wide Open, a company that specifically designs socks for wide feet—and that’s been a game changer. Instead of getting blisters in between my toes or second-guessing the wide toebox of an Altra or Topo Athletic shoe, I’ve discovered just how much socks can affect your run like Egging says.

What racing shoe options are there for wide-foot runners?

Wider width options for racing shoes are still a rarity. I’ve found through personal experience that the New Balance SuperComp Elite v6, Hoka Rocket X 3, and Hoka Cielo X1 3 have the most accommodating lasts compared to other super shoes, which taper in the midfoot resulting in narrower fit. A major thing to consider is that your feet swell over time as you run, especially on a hot day. Consider sizing up, but take into consideration most racing shoes are unisex, so they may run longer or be wider in the heel.

Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. #8865. Replacing Your Bike Chain Is Easier Than You Think—Here’s How to Do It at Home

A step-by-step home repair guide to measuring, removing, and installing a bike chain.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Replacing a chain is a great way for someone to tap into their home bike maintenance potential. It’s a pretty straightforward process once you’re used to it, especially if you have the existing chain to measure from. I typically recommend being familiar with a few skills before diving into replacing your chain. The first skill to know is adjusting your front and rear derailleurs. The second is knowing how to use a chain checker. The third is being familiar with a pre bike check. This last one is especially helpful because it will allow you to run through the bike to see if there are any other issues before diving into swapping out your chain. Again, these skills are not required skills to replace a chain, but having some familiarity with the basic mechanics addressed above will only help make this process easier. Here we’ll go through the tools you’ll need and the basic process to replace your chain at home.

How often should you replace your chain? Before answering that question, it helps to understand the process of chain wear. As your chain ages, each link’s internal bushings slowly lengthen. In turn, your now-longer chain puts added pressure on your cassette cogs and chainring teeth, causing them to wear faster. This also hampers shifting quality.

To avoid this accelerated wear of your cassette and chainrings, a general rule of thumb is to replace your bike’s chain every 2,000 miles. Mind you, this is just a starting point. No two chains will wear at exactly the same rate because no two riders treat their chains the same.

These differences in riding style are why it is best to periodically use a chain wear measuring tool to determine the condition of your chain. With the tool in hand, apply pressure to a pedal so the top of the chain is taut, and then place the measuring tool in place on the chain as shown in the video above and read the results. Indicators on the tool will tell you whether it’s time to replace your chain.

Cutting a new bike chain to the correct length for installation and removing a damaged link for an on-trail chain repair are essentially the same job. Make life easier by using a full-size tool at home, and save the compact tool for midride fixes.

To start, you’ll need to pick up the right size chain for your bike. We’re not talking about the length of the chain here (you’ll address that later), but width. This is dictated by the number of cogs on your cassette; a six-speed bike uses the same width chain as an eight-speed, but a nine-speed needs something different, and so on. (Check out Park Tool’s chain compatibility guide for more on this.) The easiest way to ensure you get the right chain is to buy the same kind of chain that came on your bike. If you decide to go with a different chain, it’s best to get one from the same manufacturer.

If your chain has a master link such as a Shimano Quick Link or SRAM PowerLock, use a pair of master link pliers to compress the link and undo it. (If it’s a newer chain, you might be able to do this with your hands.)

If there isn’t a master link, remove the chain using the chain breaker tool. Back out the tool’s pin to make room and fit a chain link into the outer slot, and line up the tool’s pin with a pin on the chain. Tighten the tool until its pin puts light pressure on the chain’s connecting pin. Crank the handle, making sure the tool’s pin stays straight. If it twists, stop and realign everything so as not to bend the tool’s pin. If you bend it, most tools have replaceable pins available; some even come with one inside the handle. Then push the pin far enough through so you can remove the extra links.

Remove the chain from your bike. Then, measure out the length of your new chain to match the length of your old chain, taking into account the master link. Remove any excess links from the new chain using the chain breaker tool, and install the master link. Thread the new chain onto your bike’s cassette and chainring and connect the ends with the master link, making sure the link is secure and locked in place.

When she’s not out riding her mountain bike, Jessica is an editor for Popular Mechanics. She was previously an editor for Bicycling magazine.
